eLife.title: Correction: Uncovering the electrical synapse proteome in retinal neurons via in vivo proximity labeling
Rhodopsin 7 is an ancestral non-canonical photoreceptor that shapes light-responsive behavior
eLife.abstract: Animals rely on light not only for vision but also to adapt behavior to their environment through non-image-forming pathways. In Drosophila, most rhodopsins mediate retinal image formation, but Rhodopsin 7 (RH7) is widely expressed in the brain and optic lobe, acting as a non-canonical light sensor reminiscent of mammalian melanopsin. We combined expression mapping, behavioral assays, and phylogenetic comparisons to investigate its function. RH7 detects temporal changes in luminance, guiding rapid behavioral responses, and regulating daily activity patterns. Flies lacking RH7 are less active during the dark phase, while strains with constitutively active RH7 show increased activity. Phylogenetic analyses suggest that RH7 is an ancient rhodopsin present across panarthropods, representing an intermediate between G protein–coupled receptors and specialized rhodopsins, highlighting a key step in the evolution of non-visual light perception. These findings show that RH7 functions as a melanopsin-like sensor, shaping behavior, and illuminating the origins of light detection.

eLife.title: A Gαq/11-IP3R1-ANO1 pacemaking axis underlies pressure-induced lymphatic chronotropy
eLife.abstract: The frequency of spontaneous lymphatic contractions is exquisitely sensitive to changes in intraluminal pressure, enabling lymph transport to be matched to the filling state of the lymphatic capillary network. The mechanistic basis of this mechanosensitive response was investigated using ex vivo contraction assays of mouse popliteal collecting vessels. Based on electrophysiological and transcriptional similarities between lymphatic muscle cells (LMCs) and arterial smooth muscle, we hypothesized that pressure-dependent chronotropy shares a parallel signaling process with pressure-induced arterial depolarization/constriction. Thus, we probed two potential mechanisms: (1) pressure-induced activation of mechanosensitive cation channels and (2) mechano-activation of GNAQ/GNA11-coupled G-protein receptors (GPCRs) that would generate second messengers to activate those channels. Contraction assays were combined with scRNA-seq analysis of the respective targets and use of transgenic mice. Our findings rule out significant roles for the mechanosensitive channels implicated in arterial myogenic constriction, as well as channels implicated in ionic pacemaking of other tissues. In contrast, smooth-muscle specific knock out or inhibition of ANO1, IP3R1, or GNAQ/GNA11 significantly abrogated pressure-induced chronotropy. These results support a scheme whereby mechano-activation of one or more GNAQ/GNA11-coupled GPCRs generates IP3, inducing sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release through IP3R1, which drives depolarization through the activation of ANO1 Cl- channels. The major GPCRs expressed in LMCs were identified and ranked by scRNAseq analysis, but individual inhibition or knock out of the top 7 candidates failed to significantly impair pressure-induced chronotropy. Our results implicate one or more GNAQ/GNA11-coupled GPCRs in mediating this mechanosensitive process, but the specific GPCRs remain to be identified.

eLife.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels
eLife.abstract: Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse’s contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

eLife.title: Human mitochondrial DNA variants influence telomere length
eLife.abstract: Telomere shortening is a hallmark of aging, yet telomere length (TL) varies considerably between individuals and is strongly influenced by inheritance. In mice, efficient mitochondrial function and low reactive oxygen species (ROS) production are essential for telomere elongation during early embryogenesis. As mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) encodes several subunits of the electron transport chain, we investigated whether mtDNA variants influence TL using a transmitochondrial cybrid model. Platelet-derived mitochondria from human donors with varying TL were introduced into mtDNA-depleted cells. Donor blood TL inversely correlated with cybrid ROS levels, suggesting that specific mtDNA variants may support telomere maintenance by enhancing mitochondrial fitness. During cybrid formation, a transient oxidative stress phase precedes cellular adaptation. At this stage, mtDNA variants associated with reduced complex I (CI) activity triggered rapid telomere shortening, which was rescued by antioxidant and NAD+ precursor supplementation. Although these variants occur naturally in some individuals with long telomeres, our findings suggest that, under conditions of acute in vitro oxidative stress, CI activity is critical for preserving telomere integrity, potentially through the regulation of NAD+/NADH balance and PARP1 activity. Overall, our findings support a role for mtDNA variation in human TL regulation and highlight potential therapeutic opportunities involving mitochondrial replacement strategies.

Water Research.title: Dynamic ice-to-water transport controls the fate of PFAS in a seasonally ice-covered lake: Integrating laboratory-derived transport rates into a modified QWASI fugacity model.
Water Research.abstract: Seasonal lake ice fundamentally alters the transport of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), but the mechanisms governing their ultimate fate remain poorly understood. In this study, we integrated field monitoring, laboratory freezing experiments, and a modified QWASI fugacity model to quantify the dynamic transport of PFOA, PFOS, PFBA, and PFBS among ice, water, and sediments in Wuliangsuhai Lake during the continuous ice-growth period. The model explicitly incorporated experimentally derived ice-to-water transport rates of PFAS together with dynamically varying ice and water volumes. Field observations showed that PFAS concentrations in ice were only 38.1-77.7% of those in under-ice water, while laboratory experiments demonstrated that the ice-to-water transport increased with the growth rate of ice and was consistently greater for PFBA and PFBS than for PFOA and PFOS. The observations agreed well with the model predictions, with relative errors not exceeding 23.05% for all of the media. Simulations suggested that long-chain PFAS were predominantly transferred to sediments through particle-associated processes, whereas short-chain PFAS remained in the aqueous phase due to enhanced ice-to-water transport and weaker particle partitioning. The findings demonstrate that the growth of lake ice reshapes PFAS transport pathways by establishing the ice-water interface as a key transport boundary governing PFAS redistribution among environmental media, thereby providing a mechanistic basis for predicting contaminant fate and environmental risks in seasonally ice-covered lakes.

Water Research.title: Component-specific roles of freshwater dissolved organic matter in regulating PFAS partitioning between water and SPM.
Water Research.abstract: The amphiphilicity of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) facilitates their transport in both the dissolved phase and suspended particulate matter (SPM). However, the effects of component-specific freshwater dissolved organic matter (DOM) on PFAS water-SPM partitioning remain poorly known. This study examined 19 PFASs and DOM components at 123 sampling sites across a sub-watershed of the lower Yangtze River, clarifying the varying impacts of fluorescent-specific DOM on the partitioning of PFASs. The findings revealed four DOM components, with microbial humic-like C1 and tryptophan-like C3 predominating, indicating strong microbial and autochthonous influences alongside spatially variable terrestrial inputs. PFASs were ubiquitous in both phases, with about one-fifth of the water-volume-equivalent burden present in the SPM on a median basis. The loading of some long-chain PFASs in SPM even exceeded those detected in the operationally dissolved phase. PFOA and PFBA dominated the dissolved phase, whereas PFHxA and PFHpS predominated in SPM; major hotspots occurred in the western and northwestern QRB. Long-chain PFASs generally exhibited stronger particle affinity, but elevated upper-tail log Kd for PFHxA and PFHpA partly weakened the overall chain-length dependence. DOM components exhibited component-specific associations with PFAS partitioning behaviors, with greater correlations observed for protein-like than humic-like components. Specifically, tryptophan-like C3 exhibited a negative association with log Kd, possibly facilitating PFAS solubility, whereas the mixed protein- and fulvic-like C4 enhanced the partitioning affinity of PFASs to SPM, likely through DOM-mediated co-sorption and colloid-particle coupling. In contrast, there was no significant correlation identified between humic-like C1/C2 and PFAS log Kd. These findings underscore the significance of considering DOM components when evaluating the behaviors and fate of PFASs in aquatic ecosystems.

Water Research.title: Thermally activated regeneration of spent LiFePO(4) with a nitrogen and phosphorus co-doped carbon layer for lithium extraction from salt-lake brine.
Water Research.abstract: Spent LiFePO4 (S-LFP) cathodes and Mg-rich salt-lake brines are conventionally handled by separate industries. Here, S-LFP powder was converted into a lithium-selective electrode for hybrid capacitive deionization (HCDI) through a two-stage thermal treatment with LiOH·H2O and discarded cooked egg yolk, which couples lithium replenishment with the growth of an N,P-co-doped carbon shell. In the optimized material, R-LFP@CNP20, the Li/Fe molar ratio recovered from 0.87 to 1.05, the heterosite FePO4 reflections disappeared, and a locally 2-4 nm carbon coating formed. In 1 M LiCl, R-LFP@CNP20 delivered 157.4 mAh g-1 at 1 C and 121.8 mAh g-1 at 10 C, showed the lowest charge-transfer resistance (1.66 Ω) and retained 92.9% of its capacity after 120 cycles at 10 C. In HCDI, it captured 6.46 mg g-1 Li+ from an 8.18 mg L⁻¹ feed with the lowest adsorption-step energy consumption of the series. It retained 70.3% of its adsorption capacity after 100 cycles and released 52.8% less Fe than S-LFP, and anode-replacement tests indicated a substantial counter-electrode contribution to full-cell decay. In Qinghai brine with a Mg/Li molar ratio of 9.9, the Li/Mg separation factor reached 7.42, and the Li fraction of the adsorbed cations increased from 9.0 to 41.2 mol%. Redirecting regenerated S-LFP to lithium extraction therefore connects spent-battery recycling with salt-lake lithium recovery, with Mg co-uptake and counter-electrode durability identified as the main remaining constraints.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: ANCHOR: AI-NGS consensus hierarchy for optimized refinement of high-affinity binders from affinity maturation
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractAffinity maturation for the systematic discovery of high-affinity protein reagents remains a major challenge in display-based protein engineering, largely because phenotypic enrichment frequently fails to correlate with true binding affinity. To improve candidate identification, we developed ANCHOR, an artificial intelligence (AI) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) consensus hierarchy for optimized refinement that implements a score-decoupled, two-stage strategy. Enrichment-trained classifier and regression models are used to construct a candidate pool, from which group-specific consensus sequences are subsequently derived without ranking candidates solely by individual model scores. Using the phosphotyrosine-binding Fyn SH2 domain as a model system, the two models achieved strong performance on untouched independent test sets (classification area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) = 0.974; regression Pearson’s r = 0.870). By leveraging a biopanning-guided filter, ANCHOR reduced the searchable sequence space by approximately four orders of magnitude while maintaining a ~90% overlap with exhaustive screening and retained 297 enrichment-predicted variants. These variants were grouped by residue identity at the least-conserved position (P4) and consensus sequences were derived within each group. Among the 16 evaluable consensus variants, 9 (56%) matched or exceeded the affinity of TrM, a previously established 100-fold-improved superbinder, with several showing a two-fold further improvement. Exploratory analyses using a structural proxy indicated robustness to parameter choices and a higher observed hit rate for ANCHOR than for the evaluated alternatives. Application to a public anti-HER2 scFv yeast-display NGS dataset demonstrated computational portability across datasets and library designs. Collectively, ANCHOR provides a practical framework for prioritizing affinity-maturation candidates from display-derived NGS data.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Rethinking long-read haplotype phasing evaluation with Phasing F1-score
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractHaplotype phasing is central to genomic analysis and molecular diagnosis because whether variants occur in cis or in trans can strongly influence their functional and clinical consequences. Although long-read sequencing has substantially improved haplotype phasing, evaluation of long-read phasing algorithms still relies on conventional metrics, including switch error rate, Hamming error rate, block NG50 and phase percentage. Here we show that these metrics have fundamental limitations: they lack direct biological or clinical interpretability, can yield ambiguous rankings, and can even be artificially optimized by methods that produce biologically uninformative results. To address these limitations, we introduce Phasing F1-score, a single interpretable metric that quantifies how accurately and completely a method recovers pairwise phase relationships between heterozygous variants, which is relevant to identifying compound heterozygosity. Phasing F1-score integrates multiple aspects of performance, including phasing accuracy, contiguity and completeness, into a single measure, enables unambiguous comparison of phasing algorithms and is robust against artificial manipulation. We further developed PIE, a parallel toolkit for efficient computation of Phasing F1-score and region-specific phasing evaluation, and used it to benchmark major long-read phasing algorithms across 38 datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio HiFi platforms. Our results show that phasing performance varies across genomic regions, highlighting the need for region-specific method selection. To support practical applications, we developed PieStore, a database for querying region-specific phasing performance and selecting the most suitable phasing algorithm. Together, this work establishes Phasing F1-score as a robust and interpretable framework for haplotype phasing evaluation and provides PieStore as a practical resource.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Hydrogen-dependent sulfur and iron reduction by marine thermophiles as analogs for early Earth and ocean world processes.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Life on the early Earth was likely anaerobic, H2 dependent, CO2 fixing, and thermophilic in a marine hydrothermal setting. Geochemical and mineral evidence suggests that sulfur and iron respiration occurred during the Paleoarchean (3.6-3.2 Ga). However, the predominant mechanisms of H2-dependent sulfur and iron respiration in hydrothermal systems, then or now, have yet to be elucidated. Studying these processes in microorganisms from modern hydrothermal systems provides context for interpreting the characteristics of life during the Paleoarchaean. All the bacteria and archaea that have been cultured and characterized as extremely thermophilic, marine, H2 dependent, and sulfur reducing or iron reducing (36 species) were surveyed for genes related to energy generation and terminal reduction processes. Respiratory hydrogenases, Nuo-like complexes, and ATP synthases were all universally conserved. These data, coupled with phenotypic and biochemical information, suggest that these organisms oxidize H2 outside the cytoplasmic membrane, reduce menaquinone, and generate a proton motive force for ATP synthesis. The most conserved sulfur reduction gene encoded a cytoplasmic NAD(P)H sulfur reductase. Genes encoding cytoplasmic hydrogenases and membrane-bound pyranopterin oxidoreductases were also common. The widespread conservation of menaquinol-dependent fumarate reductase points to CO2 assimilation as another means of electron disposal, with excess reductant possibly used to drive sulfur or iron reduction. Understanding the metabolic potential of H2-dependent marine thermophiles deepens our knowledge of life in hydrothermal systems and contributes to the interpretation of data from ocean world missions.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Comparative transcriptomics reveals the electrosynthesis mechanisms of Sporomusa ovata under different reduction potentials.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Understanding the metabolic mechanism of Sporomusa ovata is crucial for the practical applications of microbial electrosynthesis systems (MESs), a promising technology to sequester CO2. This study aims to investigate the electrosynthesis mechanisms of S. ovata under different cathodic potentials using comparative transcriptomics. As the cathodic potential became more negative from -0.4 to -0.7 V (vs standard hydrogen electrode [SHE]), acetate synthesis in MESs increased from 0.59 ± 0.05 to 6.03 ± 0.23 mM, while electron recovery efficiency decreased from 117.7 ± 6.8% to 52.5 ± 2.4%. Transcriptional analysis revealed that H2-mediated indirect extracellular electron uptake may be the core mechanism of S. ovata at -0.7 and -0.4 V. At both potentials, S. ovata relied on ATP synthesis from membrane hydrogenase-dependent respiratory chains. Compared with -0.4 V, upregulation of hydABC at -0.7 V enhanced cytoplasmic hydrogenase-based reducing power, dominating CO2 fixation via the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway. Compared with -0.7 V, the transcriptional activity of membrane hydrogenase (hupSL, hydA2B2) and higher expression of membrane electron transport components reflected the importance of the membrane-bound respiratory chain for S. ovata survival at -0.4 V. This work provides strategies for fine-tuning MESs to optimize energy efficiency and product specificity in sustainable biomanufacturing.IMPORTANCEMicrobial electrosynthesis (MES) is a promising CO2 sequestration technology and contributes to climate mitigation. Sporomusa ovata has been widely used as a cathode catalyst in MES research due to its extracellular respiratory capacity and two distinct H+-driven respiratory chains for chemolithoautotrophy. Understanding the electron transfer and metabolic mechanisms from cathodic potentials to S. ovata is important for the implementation of MES. This study demonstrated that cathodic potential regulated gene expression in S. ovata by driving metabolic switching involving energy conversion and electron transfer. In particular, expression of cytoplasmic and cytochrome b-containing hydrogenases was modulated under cathodic potentials of -0.7 and -0.4 V, respectively. The results broaden our understanding of microbial metabolic adaptation to diverse environments and provide valuable insights into how such adaptive processes can be manipulated for MES applications.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Cooperation between MIPC biosynthesis and ergosterol metabolism supports ethanol tolerance and fermentative performance in budding yeast.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: During fermentation, the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae produces and accumulates ethanol, but remains relatively tolerant despite the resulting damage to its cell surface. Complex sphingolipids and ergosterol are functionally linked in the plasma membrane and contribute to cell surface homeostasis; however, whether this relationship supports ethanol tolerance remains unclear. We previously demonstrated that biosynthesis of the complex sphingolipid mannosylinositol phosphorylceramide (MIPC) is required for cell surface adaptation to ethanol stress. Here, we investigated whether MIPC biosynthesis cooperates with ergosterol metabolism to regulate ethanol tolerance and fermentative performance. Deletion of the ergosterol biosynthetic genes ERG2 or ERG6, which function in the late stages of ergosterol biosynthesis, and repression of the squalene synthase gene ERG9 enhanced ethanol sensitivity in cells lacking MIPC biosynthesis. In contrast, deletion of SIP3, LAM1, and YSP2, which encode proteins involved in sterol transport, partially suppressed the ethanol-sensitive phenotype of cells lacking MIPC biosynthesis. Combined defects in MIPC biosynthesis and ergosterol metabolism were associated with differences in zymolyase resistance and in rhodamine 6G accumulation, suggesting altered cell surface properties in ethanol-treated cells. Furthermore, simultaneous defects in MIPC and ergosterol biosynthesis reduced cell viability and fermentative performance under high-glucose fermentation conditions. Collectively, our findings indicate that MIPC biosynthesis and ergosterol metabolism functionally cooperate to support cell surface adaptation required for ethanol tolerance and fermentative performance.IMPORTANCEProduction of alcoholic beverages and bioethanol relies on the ability of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to continue growing and fermenting as ethanol accumulates. However, ethanol damages the plasma membrane and cell wall, ultimately reducing cell viability and fermentation performance. How membrane lipids help maintain yeast cell surface integrity under ethanol stress remains incompletely understood. In this study, we show that the biosynthesis of the complex sphingolipid mannosylinositol phosphorylceramide and ergosterol metabolism function cooperatively to support cell surface adaptation to ethanol stress. Genetic defects affecting ergosterol biosynthesis further increased ethanol sensitivity when mannosylinositol phosphorylceramide biosynthesis was impaired, whereas deletion of genes involved in sterol transport partially alleviated the resulting defects. These findings establish functional cooperation between complex sphingolipids and sterols as an important mechanism supporting yeast survival and fermentation in ethanol-producing environments and suggest their potential relevance to the development of robust yeast strains for industrial fermentation.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Tracking respiratory syncytial virus dynamics in wastewater during the 2024-2025 season in Switzerland.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for a substantial health burden worldwide, particularly among children and older adults. In 2023, novel immunoprophylactic interventions for RSV were approved, underscoring the need to monitor circulating RSV lineages and detect mutations that could compromise intervention effectiveness. Here, we implemented wastewater-based genomic RSV surveillance by integrating digital PCR and amplicon-based sequencing within Switzerland's national wastewater monitoring program. We tracked RSV subtypes and individual mutations across the 2024-2025 peak season in six Swiss cities. RSV-A and RSV-B co-circulated nationwide, and both exhibited similar epidemiological dynamics estimated from their subtype-specific effective reproduction numbers. No previously reported F protein mutations relevant to prophylaxis efficacy were identified. Genetic diversity analysis of wastewater-derived sequences reflected patterns previously reported in clinical data, with higher diversity in RSV-A than RSV-B, and greater variability in the G compared to the F gene. These findings demonstrate the potential of wastewater-based RSV surveillance for monitoring RSV dynamics and diversity and establish a national baseline for RSV evolution during the first season following vaccine implementation in Switzerland.IMPORTANCERespiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common respiratory virus that can cause serious illness in vulnerable populations. The recent development of RSV immunoprophylaxis products has increased the importance of monitoring viral evolution. Standard surveillance based on clinical testing captures only a fraction of infections. Our findings demonstrate that wastewater-based genomic surveillance, using regularly collected samples throughout the peak RSV season, can provide a cost-effective and representative picture of viral dynamics. Expanding this approach into future RSV seasons and across a broader geographic scope will enable continuous tracking of viral evolution, including detection of novel mutations, which is particularly important given the widespread introduction of new vaccines and preventive treatments.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: The quorum-sensing SinI/SinR-TraI/TraR/SinR systems upregulate the lead immobilization-related genes and metabolites involved in cell wall/membrane components and sulfur metabolism in Ensifer adhaerens S24.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The quorum-sensing SinI/SinR-TraI/TraR/SinR systems (STIRSS) in Ensifer adhaerens S24 promote lead (Pb) immobilization via cell surface adsorption and extracellular precipitation; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. Here, the molecular mechanisms underlying the STIRSS-regulated Pb immobilization by S24 were explored in a Pb-polluted solution. Transcriptomic analysis revealed significantly downregulated expression of Pb immobilization-related genes involved in fatty acid metabolism (gene1765, fabF, and fabI), cell wall/membrane components (omp31, lptC, and pldB), sulfur metabolism, and hydrogen sulfide biosynthesis (cysU, cysP, pA_gene0512, cysW, and cysZ) in the ∆sinI/R-traI/R/sinR compared with that in S24. Metabolomic analysis demonstrated downregulated expression of intracellular metabolites involved in fatty acids, cell wall/membrane components, and sulfur amino acids in the ∆sinI/R-traI/R/sinR compared with that in S24. Real-time reverse transcription-quantitative PCR analysis showed downregulated expression of pA_gene0512, cysW, fabI, fabF, cysU, cysP, cysZ, and omp31 in the ∆sinI/R-traI/R/sinR compared with that in S24 under Pb-free and Pb-added conditions. Furthermore, the solution Pb concentrations were significantly increased in the presence of the ∆cysW, ∆cysZ, ∆pA_gene0512, ∆fabF, and ∆fabI compared with those in the presence of S24 after 20 h of incubation. These findings suggest that the STIRSS in S24 enhance Pb immobilization by upregulating the expression of various genes and intracellular metabolites involved in cell surface adsorption and extracellular Pb precipitation in Pb-contaminated solutions. Our results provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying QS STIRSS-regulated Pb immobilization by E. adhaerens S24. [IMPORTANCE] To date, the molecular mechanisms underlying Pb immobilization by heavy metal-immobilizing bacteria remain poorly understood. This study characterizes the molecular mechanisms involved in the QS SinI/SinR-TraI/TraR/SinR systems (STIRSS)-regulated Pb immobilization by E. adhaerens S24 in a Pb-polluted solution. The STIRSS significantly increased the expression of genes and intracellular metabolites involved in fatty acid metabolism, cell wall/membrane components, sulfur amino acids, sulfate transport, and hydrogen sulfide biosynthesis, contributing to Pb immobilization by S24. Furthermore, the addition of Pb induced the expression of the STIRSS-regulated genes (fabI, fabF, cysW, cysZ, omp31, and pA_gene0512) involved in fatty acid metabolism, cell wall/membrane components, and H2S production in S24. Our results provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms that the QS STIRSS facilitate Pb immobilization by bacteria. Our results may serve as a crucial foundation for employing QS regulation to enhance the efficiency of Pb removal by heavy metal-immobilizing bacteria in Pb-polluted aquatic environments for environmental remediation applications.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Sheep or cattle fecal contamination? Using long-read amplicon sequencing for fecal source attribution and apportionment.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Fecal contamination of freshwater poses a risk to environmental and human health. Accurately attributing contamination to specific sources is critical for remediation. However, discriminating between closely related ruminants, sheep and cattle, remains a challenge. This study evaluated the use of fast expectation maximization microbial source tracking (FEAST) and mitochondrial and microbial source tracking (MST) qPCR markers for fecal source identification. The focus was differentiation between cattle and sheep sources using a spiked laboratory experiment with known fecal inputs and field testing of samples from an agricultural stream. Sheep and cattle fecal samples were diluted into urban stream water, with spiked samples containing either single or mixed feces at varying ratios. Field samples were collected from a rural stream where adjacent sheep and cattle grazed. Full-length 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of spiked fecal and field samples was conducted, and the resulting taxonomies were used as input to FEAST; the results were also compared with those of MST analysis. Single cattle or sheep fecal sources could be identified by FEAST, but thresholds need to be established to avoid misattribution. FEAST results for field samples were consistent with ruminant and cattle MST markers, but the low sensitivity of cattle/sheep MST markers complicated comparisons. Using taxonomic groupings for FEAST analysis gave greater discrimination. However, apportionment of source contributions was not consistent within groupings. Inclusion of an aquatic source reduced misattribution of non-fecal microflora to animal sources. FEAST is a promising tool for source tracking but struggles to differentiate between mixed sources with similar fecal microflora and to produce accurate source apportionment.IMPORTANCEFecal contamination of freshwater is an issue for communities across the world because it has both environmental and health consequences. Therefore, differentiating between potential sources of contamination is important for both remediation and risk assessment. Microbes from fecal material are one of the main indicators used to track fecal contamination and identify its potential sources. In recent years, the use of the entire gut microflora to determine the origins of fecal contamination events has become a promising area of research and has the potential to overcome the low sensitivity of ruminant host-associated MST markers in field samples. The research demonstrated that an algorithm developed for this purpose could identify contamination from single sources. However, when applied to mixed-source scenarios, it struggled to differentiate between the similar microflora of livestock ruminants, cattle and sheep. Inclusion of an aquatic source was important for reducing misattribution of non-fecal microflora to animal sources.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Simultaneous quantification of DMSP-related sulfur metabolites reveals hidden metabolic diversity in marine bacteria.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) is a key organosulfur compound in marine ecosystems, and its microbial metabolism involves multiple biosynthetic and degradative pathways that are difficult to fully resolve using conventional stepwise approaches. In this study, we developed a targeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) method for the simultaneous quantification of six key DMSP-related sulfur metabolites in a single analysis, including L-methionine (L-Met), S-methyl-L-methionine (SMM), 4-methylthio-2-hydroxybutyrate (MTHB), 3-methylthiopropylamine (MTPA), 3-methylmercaptopropionate (MMPA), and DMSP. The method was validated over the concentration range of 0.1-1,500 ng/mL and showed good specificity, linearity, precision, accuracy, extraction recovery, matrix effects, and stability. Its applicability was assessed in the model DMSP-degrading strain Ruegeria pomeroyi DSS-3 and the DMSP-producing strain Roseibium aggregatum LZB033, where time-course experiments captured metabolite dynamics consistent with their established pathways. Application to 42 marine bacterial isolates identified metabolite profiles consistent with PCR detection of known DMSP metabolic genes, as well as unexpected patterns in strains for which the corresponding genes were not amplified. These included MMPA accumulation after DMSP supplementation without detectable dmdA amplification, the co-occurrence of MTPA, MMPA, and DMSP without amplification of the screened DMSP biosynthesis genes, and high MMPA levels after L-Met supplementation without detectable DMSP. These findings highlight potential metabolic routes that warrant further investigation. Collectively, this metabolite-guided LC-MS/MS method offers a rapid and integrated tool for characterizing bacterial DMSP-related metabolic phenotypes, and identifying candidate pathways for further genetic and biochemical characterization.IMPORTANCEDimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) is one of the most abundant organic sulfur compounds in the ocean, and an important component of marine sulfur cycling. Marine bacteria transform DMSP through diverse metabolic pathways, but these pathways remain difficult to fully resolve because metabolites are often analyzed individually. We developed a rapid analytical approach that simultaneously measures six DMSP-related sulfur metabolites, providing a more complete view of bacterial sulfur metabolism. Applying this approach to diverse marine bacteria revealed metabolic patterns that could not be explained by currently known pathways. In several strains, sulfur compounds accumulated despite the absence of expected metabolic genes, pointing to previously unrecognized routes of DMSP metabolism. Our findings demonstrate that marine bacteria possess greater sulfur metabolic diversity than currently appreciated and provide a new approach for uncovering hidden pathways in marine sulfur cycling.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Ligilactobacillus salivarius inhibits GII.4[P16] human norovirus replication in zebrafish larvae.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Human gut bacteria can modulate human norovirus (HuNoV) infection, underscoring the need to characterize virus-bacterium interactions. This study evaluated the effect of Ligilactobacillus salivarius on HuNoV GII.4[P16] replication using a zebrafish larva model. A GII.4[P16]-positive stool specimen was resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), centrifuged, and the supernatant stored at -80°C. L. salivarius was grown overnight in de Man, Rogosa, and Sharpe broth, from which bacterial cells and cell-free supernatant (CFS) were collected. The overnight broth (OB), cells, and CFS were each mixed with virus suspension at a 1:1 ratio, and 3 nL were microinjected into 3-day post-fertilization larvae; controls received PBS with virus. Daily until 4 days post-infection (dpi), 2 samples of 10 pooled larvae were collected, and RNA was extracted and quantified by droplet digital PCR. Two-way analysis of variance showed that treatment and time significantly influenced viral RNA levels (P < 0.001), with a marginal interaction (P = 0.051) indicating consistent inhibitory trends across the study period. CFS-injected larvae showed replication comparable to controls (P > 0.05), peaking at 5.31 log RNA copies/larva at 1 dpi, whereas cell-containing treatments (cells and OB) significantly reduced replication (P < 0.01) throughout the 4-day period. An in vitro binding assay showed that 67% of the virus inoculum physically bound to L. salivarius. In a further comparison, both live and heat-killed bacteria reduced replication initially; live L. salivarius significantly inhibited replication at 3 dpi (P < 0.05). These findings support the hypothesis that L. salivarius physically binds to HuNoV GII.4[P16] and inhibits viral replication, highlighting its potential as a probiotic intervention for HuNoV infection.IMPORTANCENorovirus remains the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide, responsible for nearly 700 million cases and substantial economic burden annually, yet no vaccine or antiviral therapy currently exists. This study's findings are significant because they identify a specific probiotic strain, Ligilactobacillus salivarius, capable of directly binding to and inhibiting replication of a clinically relevant norovirus genotype (GII.4[P16]), which is responsible for many recent outbreaks globally. By demonstrating that live bacterial cells-not just secreted metabolites-drive this antiviral effect, the study points toward a mechanistic, cell-mediated mode of action that could inform targeted probiotic formulations. The use of a zebrafish larva model also offers a valuable, scalable in vivo system for studying norovirus-microbiome interactions, addressing a major bottleneck in norovirus research caused by the lack of robust cell culture systems. Together, these findings advance understanding of bacterium-virus interactions and support further development of probiotic-based strategies for preventing or reducing norovirus infection severity.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Putative conjugative transfer and persistence of carbapenem resistance gene bla(OXA-72) from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRA) has been associated with increased morbidity and mortality in clinical settings. In this study, we explored the transfer potential of a mobilizable plasmid-harboring blaOXA-72 gene between Acinetobacter species originating from patients, municipal wastewater, and pig farm wastewater. PCR-based evidence suggested putative transfer of blaOXA-72 from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii. In this pair, the apparent frequency of PCR-marker-positive putative transconjugants varied depending on temperature and meropenem supplementation, with a higher frequency observed at 27°C than at 17°C and 37°C. Likewise, the presence of antibiotic pressure yielded a higher apparent conjugation frequency; however, this observation was limited to a single donor-recipient pair. Further, we revealed a phenotypic conversion in terms of meropenem susceptibility and a fitness cost in the putative transconjugants. While whole-genome sequencing did not conclusively verify the presence of blaOXA-72 or a fully resolved plasmid configuration, Oxford Nanopore read mapping consistently detected the chromosomal strA gene in all isolates. In contrast, only a limited number of reads aligned with the blaOXA-72 gene, traC, or the complete plasmid sequences. Comparative analyses further revealed variations in the composition of surface-associated factors and defense systems of the recipient strains, which could be considered as barriers to conjugation. Lastly, the persistence of PCR-detectable marker genes in putative transconjugants was variable and generally unstable over a 30-day period. Overall, these findings provide preliminary insights into the factors that may influence horizontal gene transfer and short-term maintenance of blaOXA-72.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRA) is a serious clinical concern linked to elevated morbidity and mortality. This study shed light on how the carbapenemase gene blaOXA-72 spreads in the environment via horizontal gene transfer. Using isolates of Acinetobacter pittii and Acinetobacter baumannii from municipal wastewater treatment plants, we show that PCR-based evidence of putative conjugative transfer of the blaOXA-72 gene depends on temperature and antibiotic exposure. The process also incurs fitness costs, and the transferred gene persists only briefly in recipient cells. These results emphasize the importance of environmental sources as reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance gene exchange. Additionally, variations in surface structures and defense systems may act as potential barriers to conjugation. Overall, the work improves our understanding of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) movement and supports the need for better integrated surveillance under a One Health approach.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: A temperate phage acts as a symbiotic fitness enhancer for UPEC but surrenders to combination therapy through lysogeny suppression.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Temperate phages are increasingly recognized as key drivers of bacterial evolution. Here, we isolated a myoviral prophage, vB_EcoM_P899, from a clinical uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) isolate and characterized how lysogenization shapes host biology. Lysogenization significantly enhanced biofilm formation, swarming motility, oxidative stress resistance, and adhesion to macrophages (up to 100-fold) without altering antibiotic susceptibility or overall 72-h lethality in the Galleria mellonella larval infection model. Mechanistically, this is associated with upregulation of the fimbrial gene FimA and enhanced inducibility of the oxidative stress response genes KatE and OxyR under oxidative stress. Crucially, combining P899 with ciprofloxacin or kanamycin produced synergistic killing and suppressed new lysogen formation in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. In contrast, ceftazidime, while synergistic, failed to prevent lysogeny. Our findings demonstrate that while prophage vB_EcoM_P899 promotes bacterial niche adaptation, its lysogenization frequency is significantly reduced under specific antibiotic pressure, facilitating clearance of the challenged UPEC population. This work provides a strong rationale for optimizing phage-antibiotic combination therapies to treat drug-resistant infections by simultaneously enhancing bacterial killing and limiting lysogenic survivors. [IMPORTANCE] This study reveals that lysogenization by a temperate phage can enhance the niche adaptation of uropathogenic Escherichia coli without increasing its virulence in the Galleria mellonella larval model or altering antibiotic resistance. Crucially, we demonstrate that combining this phage with select antibiotics (e.g., kanamycin and ciprofloxacin) not only kills the bacteria effectively but also actively suppresses the formation of new lysogens in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. These findings uncover a novel role for temperate phages as symbiotic regulators within the host and provide direct experimental evidence for a phage-antibiotic combination strategy. This approach holds promise for combating chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections and offers a clinically viable pathway to address antibiotic tolerance in chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Decoding microbial diversity in roots of rice plants under flooded conditions: influence of the host genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal association.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Rice is a vital staple for more than half of the world's population, uniquely adapted to grow under flooded conditions. Our current understanding of root-associated microbiomes in rice plants under flooded conditions (anaerobic rice) is, however, limited. While rice plants are capable of establishing symbiotic associations with arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi, also under flooded conditions, little is known about the impact that mycorrhizal associations might have on the root microbiome. Here, we used metagenomic sequencing to characterize the root-associated microbiomes of cultivated rice grown under flooded conditions. The root endosphere and rhizosphere compartments were found to harbor distinct microbial communities, with bacterial taxa comprising approximately 95% of the total microbial community. At the phylum level, the root bacteriome was primarily composed of Pseudomonadota (Alphaproteobacteria, Betaproteobacteria, and Gammaproteobacteria), followed by Actinomycetota. The fungal microbiome was dominated by Ascomycota (Sordariomycetes, Eurotiomycetes, and Dothideomycetes) and Basidiomycota. Both root compartment and host genotype significantly influenced microbiome composition, with most genotype-specific recruitment occurring at the species level. These associations were further reshaped in plants pre-inoculated with the AM fungus Rhizophagus irregularis. Co-occurrence networks revealed a genotype-dependent effect in the complexity of microbial taxa in mycorrhizal rice plants. Key microbial species primarily involved in methane production and nutrient cycling (e.g., phosphate-solubilizing bacteria and nitrogen-cycling bacteria) residing in roots of flooded rice were identified. Functional analysis of gene abundance related to those microbial communities revealed compartmentalization, with nutrient-cycling bacteria being more prevalent at the endosphere. Overall, this study demonstrated that the rice genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal condition shape the root microbiome in rice plants, ultimately influencing holobiont dynamics in flooded rice fields. [IMPORTANCE] Plant roots harbor a large diversity of microorganisms that strongly influence plant health and improve stress tolerance. Among them, root colonization by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi enhances mineral nutrition and mitigates environmental stress. Although most rice cultivated worldwide is grown under anaerobic conditions (flooded fields), investigation of microbial communities inhabiting root-associated compartments of flooded rice, including AM fungi, has received only little attention. Here, we demonstrated that the rice genotype, root compartment, and mycorrhizal condition markedly influence the microbiome in roots of rice plants in flooded conditions, thus illustrating the potential of the rice plant to shape its root-associated microbiome. Differential root-associated microbiomes of commercial rice varieties include microbes primarily associated with methane production and nutrient cycling. Elucidation of factors influencing root-associated microbiomes in flooded rice systems, including their association with AM fungi, offers practical guidance for exploiting root-associated microbial communities for sustainable rice cultivation while reducing reliance on agrochemicals.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Advancing NTM research with citizen science.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) is a generic term for the >200 species of environmental mycobacteria. NTM are ubiquitous, but there is extensive variation in the distribution of individual species. In a recent article published in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, Wilsey et al. describe how community-based citizen science efforts helped map the distribution of NTM in Hawai'i (R. N. Wilsey, L.-H. Ding, S. N. Dawrs, C. K. Raulerson, et al., Appl Environ Microbiol 92:e00269-26, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.00269-26). Mycobacterium chimaera, an opportunistic pathogen and the leading cause of NTM pulmonary disease in Hawai'i, was among the most common species isolated.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: A putative GtrB-like glycosyltransferase modulates cation-dependent BCP8-2 phage infection and cell surface structure in Bacillus cereus.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Bacillus cereus is a foodborne pathogen of growing concern due to its persistence and antimicrobial resistance. To identify host determinants influencing susceptibility to phage BCP8-2, a mini-Tn10 transposon mutant library of B. cereus ATCC 14579 was constructed and screened for altered phage susceptibility. A mutant (BC2012) showing partial resistance carried an insertion in BC_RS27090 (previously BC_5432), encoding a putative GtrB-like bactoprenol glycosyltransferase. Complementation restored phage sensitivity, confirming its functional involvement. The mutant showed a slight reduction in efficiency of plating, whereas, adsorption assay revealed significantly reduced phage binding and infectivity, particularly under cation-rich conditions. Furthermore, adsorption kinetics and one-step growth curve in mutant supported that gtrB mutation affects initial adsorption. Microscopy showed altered surface morphology with thinner, smoother cell walls. These data indicate that gtrB affects surface properties essential for cation-dependent phage adsorption and infection and provide a foundation for future studies on the role of surface glycosylation and ionic interactions in Gram-positive phage biology.IMPORTANCEPathogenic Bacillus cereus is resilient across diverse environments and produces diverse toxins linked to foodborne outbreaks. Bacteriophages provide an effective strategy to control B. cereus; however, molecular targets of phage-host interaction are poorly understood, limiting the effective phage-based control. The current study addresses this gap by identifying a putative bactoprenol glycosyltransferase (GtrB), a viral factor in phage BCP8-2 susceptibility. Data obtained highlight a partial reduction of phage infection in the gtrB mutant, demonstrating that GtrB-like glycosyltransferase significantly contributes to BCP8-2 phage infection and adsorption. Our findings provide significant insights into advancing phage therapy, antibiotic resistance, and B. cereus biocontrol in food and clinical settings.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Development of improved host-vector system for enhanced production of santalene isoforms in Azospirillum brasilense.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Azospirillum brasilense is a non-photosynthetic bacterium that possesses the ability to produce carotenoids, in which squalene is a critical intermediate of the carotenoid biosynthetic pathway. Farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) serves as a precursor for the production of sesquiterpenoids; hence, its availability is a major bottleneck in the microbial biosynthesis of several major plant sesquiterpenes. We improved the utility of A. brasilense Cd for the heterologous production of sesquiterpenes by enhancing intracellular availability of FPP and disrupted the chromosomal hpnC gene to block the squalene biosynthetic pathway to decrease a competing sink for FPP, along with the introduction of the heterologous Escherichia coli ispA gene, together with additional copies of the native A. brasilense dxps and crtE genes. These genetic manipulations, along with the expression of codon-harmonized santalene synthase from Santalum album, enabled an increase in the production of α-santalene by 50-fold, α-exo-bergamotene by 20-fold, and β-santalene by 10-fold in A. brasilense Cd. Additionally, we developed a fructose-inducible santalene synthase expression system, which may be more efficient and economical than the isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside-inducible system. Finally, by cloning and expressing genes encoding cytochrome P450 monooxygenase and its cognate NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, we have shown the potential of A. brasilense to produce santalols, the most desired ingredient of sandalwood oil.IMPORTANCESandalwood oil is among the most valuable natural fragrances and is also known for its diverse biological activities. The biosynthesis of santalene, a major constituent of sandalwood oil, originates from the universal precursors isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) via the MEP pathway. This pathway is naturally present in Azospirillum brasilense, a plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium, making it a suitable host for the heterologous production of sesquiterpenes. This study has shown the possibility of using A. brasilense as a promising host-vector system for enhancing the production of santalene isomers by several fold. It has also shown the superiority of a fructose-inducible system over the isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside-inducible system for the industrial production of high-value secondary metabolites in this bacterium.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: A cryptic lactate cycle in CO fermentation by Clostridium ljungdahlii.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The valorization of C1 gases presents a route toward the utilization of industrial waste gases as resources. Acetogens such as Clostridium ljungdahlii serve as promising microbial cell factories for light-independent carbon fixation and high-value compound production, yet their efficiency is often limited by energy constraints and poorly understood metabolic pathways. Here, we investigated lactate metabolism in C. ljungdahlii during carbon monoxide (CO) fermentation via growth and product profiling, 13C-labeling, gene knockouts, and transcriptomics. Although lactate cannot serve as the sole source of carbon and energy for C. ljungdahlii's growth, we found that lactate can be co-fermented with CO into acetate. 13C-tracing further revealed concurrent lactate production and oxidation during CO fermentation, with the unlabeled lactate fraction increasing from 1.0% (day 2) to 5.0% (day 6), indicating the existence of an active lactate cycle. Genetic and transcriptional analyses showed that lactate production and oxidation were catalyzed by two distinct lactate dehydrogenases: LdhA (CLJU_RS15865) and the electron-bifurcating Ldh/EtfAB_1 complex (CLJU_RS10590-CLJU_RS10600), respectively. Disruption of the lactate cycle, particularly in the Ldh/EtfAB_1 mutant, improved energy metabolism and triggered intracellular metabolic rearrangements. This mutant produced approximately 10-fold more lactate and shifted the acetate/ethanol ratio from 3.7:1 to 2.1:1, accompanied by upregulation of the AOR (aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductase)-mediated ethanol production pathway. Subsequent ldhA overexpression further elevated lactate titer to ~2.5 mM, confirming the potential for lactate production from CO. The results imply that the cryptic lactate cycle dissipates energy but aids in intracellular redox balancing during CO fermentation. These findings provide new insights into the metabolic engineering of acetogens to produce target compounds, such as lactate and ethanol. [IMPORTANCE] Acetogens possess a natural carbon fixation pathway, the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, enabling them to fix CO or CO2 to produce acetate. Among various acetogens, Clostridium ljungdahlii exhibits strong tolerance to CO and thus holds great application potential for the resource utilization of syngas. However, the physiological and metabolic mechanisms underlying its autotrophic fermentation remain incompletely understood, which imposes limitations on metabolic engineering efforts. In this study, we systematically investigated lactate metabolism in C. ljungdahlii and revealed the existence of a cryptic lactate cycle during CO fermentation. By characterizing this cycle's operation and its impacts on energy metabolism and carbon distribution, we elucidated its potential physiological functions. These findings not only expand our understanding of the physiological and metabolic behaviors of acetogens during autotrophic fermentation but also provide theoretical guidance for the future metabolic engineering of lactate, ethanol, and other compounds.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: AspA activity orchestrates a growth-stress survival trade-off in Yersinia pestis via metabolic reprogramming.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: The aspA gene of Yersinia pestis exhibits a pronounced polymorphism at codon 363, with the dominant TTG allele encoding an inactive aspartate ammonia-lyase (AspA) while the GTG allele encoding an active enzyme. We previously demonstrated that this polymorphism drives an environment-dependent fitness trade-off, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. To address this, we first characterized the phenotypic differences between the two strains and revealed a clear growth-stress survival trade-off: the GTG (AspA-active) strain grew faster and produced more ATP, whereas the TTG (AspA-inactive) strain, despite slower growth, exhibited superior survival under nutrient limitation with oxidative, anaerobic, or hyperosmotic stress. Exogenous aspartate reversed the GTG strain's disadvantages under anaerobic or cold stress. To dissect the metabolic basis, we performed 13C-labeled metabolic flux analysis on these two strains. The GTG strain rapidly converted aspartate to fumarate via AspA, fueling the TCA cycle and boosting ATP production. In contrast, the TTG strain displayed stalled aspartate utilization and accumulated amino acids and lipids. Supplementation with TCA cycle intermediates (fumarate, succinate, or malate) partially rescued TTG growth, confirming that reduced TCA flux limits its proliferation. Collectively, AspA activity orchestrates a growth-stress survival trade-off through metabolic reprogramming, underlying the antagonistic pleiotropy of Y. pestis in aspartate-available or stressful environments. The "metabolic congestion" strategy of the TTG strain enhances survival under multiple stresses relevant to the flea gut, and it is plausible that this metabolic reprogramming may contribute to transmission and provide a selective advantage under flea-borne conditions.IMPORTANCEThe plague bacterium Yersinia pestis encounters oxidative, anaerobic, and hyperosmotic stresses-conditions relevant to its flea gut environment during transmission. This study reveals that a single, naturally occurring polymorphism in the aspA gene shifts the bacterium's metabolism from a growth-focused mode to a "metabolic congestion" state that enhances survival under these stresses in vitro. Our work provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how metabolic reprogramming could influence adaptation to vector-like conditions, offering a plausible basis for the environment-dependent fitness trade-offs that may shape transmission dynamics.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Anaerobic microorganisms alter heavy oil chemistry by oxygenation and sulfurization.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Microbial transformation of heavy oil under anoxic conditions involves complex changes in hydrocarbon and heteroatom-containing molecular compositions. However, the molecular-level evolution of sulfur-containing compounds and their relationship to hydrocarbon transformation remain insufficiently resolved. In this study, long-term anaerobic microcosms containing heavy oil from Pitch Lake, Trinidad and Tobago, were analyzed using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) and microbial community profiling to evaluate temporal changes in molecular compositions and microbiota structure over 945 days of incubation. FT-ICR MS detected 4,499 molecular formulas dominated by CHO-, CHNO-, CHOS-, and CHNOS-class formulas. Pronounced compositional shifts occurred during incubation, with sulfur-containing molecular formulas becoming increasingly abundant and resulting in a marked increase in CHOS-class formulas over time. Intensity-weighted elemental formulas showed increasing oxygen and sulfur abundances, while the average m/z increased from 344 at day 93 to 366 at day 945, corresponding to an approximately 6.4% increase in the intensity-weighted average molecular mass. Multivariate analyses revealed distinct temporal clustering of samples and parallel shifts in microbial community composition, depicting a greater contribution of anaerobic and sulfur-associated taxa. Correlation analyses further showed associations between microbial community shifts and increasing abundances of oxidized sulfur-containing compounds, particularly CHSO3- and CHSO4-class formulas. These findings indicate substantial reorganization of the heteroatom-containing molecular pool during anoxic incubation and highlight the potential roles of microbial and sulfur-related processes in the transformation of heavy oil under anoxic conditions.IMPORTANCEHeavy oil reservoirs contain complex mixtures of hydrocarbons and heteroatom-containing compounds that undergo transformation under anoxic conditions. Characterizing the molecular-level changes occurring during these transformations is important for understanding hydrocarbon biodegradation, the persistence of recalcitrant compounds, and the formation and fate of organic sulfur species in oil reservoirs. Using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) and microbial community analyses, this study reveals that long-term anaerobic incubation drives enrichment of CHOS-class formulas, reduced microbial diversity, and shifts toward anaerobic, sulfur-associated taxa. These findings demonstrate that microbial and sulfur-driven processes play a key role in reorganizing oil chemistry and suggest that co-metabolic activity contributes to the accumulation of partially transformed sulfur-containing compounds. By directly linking changes in microbial community composition with ultrahigh-resolution molecular characterization, this work provides important new insights into the microbial and chemical mechanisms controlling heavy oil transformation and sulfur metabolism in subsurface oil reservoirs.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Acetate scavenging and aromatic funneling of lignocellulose-derived carbon in the denitrifier Pseudomonas veronii.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Lignocellulose degradation and denitrification frequently co-occur in soils and sediments with fluctuating or limited O2 availability, yet the ability of facultative denitrifiers to couple aromatic carbon turnover to nitrate respiration remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized a novel isolate, Pseudomonas veronii strain B19, for its genetic potential and physiological performance during growth on hemicellulose- and lignin-derived substrates under oxic and denitrifying conditions. Genome analysis revealed extensive aromatic catabolic pathways, including a complete β-ketoadipate route funneling lignin-derived compounds to central metabolism. Despite lacking classical endo-xylanases, the strain grew on acetylated xylan, with faster denitrification kinetics than on glucose. Proteomic and electron flow analyses indicate that xylan utilization proceeds via deacetylation and acetate assimilation through acetyl-CoA. Notably, the carbon source governed the denitrification regulatory phenotype: glucose elicited bet hedging and transient nitrite accumulation at the oxic-anoxic transition, whereas xylan-derived acetate supported a seamless transition to denitrification. On alkali-solubilized lignin, the strain utilized soluble monoaromatic compounds under both oxic and denitrifying conditions. Oxic metabolism proceeded through strong induction of O2-dependent mono- and dioxygenases, enabling extensive aromatic catabolism, whereas under denitrifying conditions, conversion was only partial, with vanillate accumulation and electron-limited but stoichiometrically efficient nitrate reduction at minimal N2O formation. Together, these findings demonstrate that B19 links lignocellulose-derived carbon turnover to denitrification under limited O2, prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Its preference for soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin fractions and converging catabolic pathways indicate a role in downstream turnover of already-depolymerized lignin-derived aromatics, consistent with biological funneling and relevant to lignin valorization.IMPORTANCEDenitrification and the breakdown of plant-derived carbon are central to nitrogen and carbon cycling in soils and sediments, yet how these processes intersect when oxygen is scarce is poorly understood. Most denitrifiers are thought to rely on simple carbon sources, while the breakdown of polymeric lignin is considered oxygen-dependent. Here, we show that the facultative anaerobe Pseudomonas veronii B19 couples the turnover of acetylated hemicellulose and soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin-derived aromatics to denitrification, sustaining respiration under oxygen limitation by prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Notably, the carbon source itself dictated the organism's denitrification behavior, switching it between distinct regulatory strategies. By resolving these mechanisms in a single isolate, this work clarifies how facultative denitrifiers may process depolymerized plant carbon and shape nitrogen gas emissions in oxygen-limited environments, and identifies traits relevant to the downstream microbial valorization of lignin-derived aromatics.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Combined application of Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains and zinc suppresses Alternaria alternata leaf spot in chili pepper.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Chili pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) is a vital vegetable crop susceptible to yield loss from Alternaria alternata (Fr.), Keissl., which causes leaf spot/blight and fruit rot. Harnessing beneficial rhizobacteria offers an eco-friendly strategy to enhance plant resilience to biotic stressors. In vitro screening identified Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains viz., P. chlororaphis subsp. aurantiaca (ARS-38) and P. chlororaphis subsp. chlororaphis (RP-4) as potent antifungal strains, inhibiting A. alternata growth by 62% and 64%, respectively. In a zinc (Zn)-amended medium, their antifungal activity increased further, reducing fungal growth by 70% with individual strains and 93% when combined. Microscopy revealed fungal growth inhibition linked to conidia and conidiophore disintegration. In planta under open-field pot conditions, A. alternata infection resulted in 100% disease incidence (DI) and altered histochemical, photosynthetic, and enzyme responses. Treatment with ARS-38 + RP-4 in Zn-amended soil enhanced plant resistance by increasing lignin and phenolic accumulation and reducing enzyme activities, resulting in a 96% reduction in DI. Zinc supplementation improved plant health and enhanced disease suppression when combined with the bacterial strains. Combining rhizobacteria with Zn (2 mg/kg) emerges as a promising strategy to mitigate Alternaria leaf spot disease and enhance biostress tolerance in chili plants. [IMPORTANCE] Biological control offers a sustainable approach for reducing fungal diseases while limiting reliance on chemical fungicides. This study shows that two Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains, ARS-38 and RP-4, combined with low-level zinc supplementation, strongly suppress Alternaria alternata, an important chili pepper pathogen. The combined treatment reduced fungal growth in vitro and substantially decreased disease development in plants while improving structural, physiological, and biochemical responses associated with plant health. The findings demonstrate the potential value of integrating beneficial rhizobacteria with micronutrient supplementation for sustainable disease management and provide a basis for further development of microbial-micronutrient strategies for crop protection.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Oxidation of Fe(II) by nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizers enriched from Fe(III)-rich microbial mats of an extreme acidic river (Río Tinto, Spain).
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizing (NRFeOx) microorganisms have been detected in the subsurface of the Iberian Pyrite Belt (Spain), where the Río Tinto originates. However, it is not known whether NRFeOx microorganisms are present in the Fe(III)-rich microbial mats that developed within the surface waters where the river originates, and the geochemical conditions progressively shift from circumneutral to highly acidic. Moreover, it is not known what the main (microbial) Fe(II) oxidation pathway is under in situ pH conditions. To answer these questions, we (i) analyzed the in situ bacterial community and Fe mineralogy of the Fe(III)-rich microbial mats, (ii) set up NRFeOx enrichment cultures (either with NO3-/Fe2+aq or acetate/NO3-/Fe2+aq), and (iii) evaluated denitrification and Fe(II) oxidation capabilities of the NRFeOx enrichments under in situ pH conditions. We found that the microbial mat was composed mainly of poorly crystalline minerals, such as ferrihydrite and schwertmannite, with the microaerophilic Fe(II)-oxidizing genus Gallionella (18.3% ± 4.9% DNA-based and 10.8% ± 1.9% RNA-based relative 16S rRNA [gene] abundances) being the main bacteria present and active. NRFeOx was only observed in the enrichment culture amended with acetate/NO3-/Fe2+aq, where Rhodoblastus (between 73.1% and 91.0% DNA-based) was the main enriched genus. The production of nitrite in the Rhodoblastus-dominated culture suggested that chemodenitrification, i.e., the abiotic oxidation of Fe(II) by nitrite, was the main Fe(II) oxidation pathway at pH between 6.2 and 7. However, under more acidic conditions (pH 5.8), nitrate reduction still occurred without Fe(II) oxidation. Overall, this study suggests that NRFeOx microorganisms present in the Río Tinto microbial mats may couple NO3- reduction to Fe(II) oxidation in anoxic circumneutral microniches where nitrate and organic carbon are also available.IMPORTANCEThe potential role of nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizing (NRFeOx) microorganisms in subsurface pyrite weathering and the formation of acid mine drainage environments, such as the Río Tinto river, is still poorly understood. By focusing on Fe(III)-rich microbial mats formed at the interface between anoxic Fe(II)-rich groundwater and oxic conditions, this study addresses how NRFeOx microorganisms contribute to nitrogen, iron, and carbon cycling in this acidic environment. Moreover, identifying and enriching NRFeOx microorganisms adapted to low pH can deepen our understanding of their metabolic versatility and resilience. These insights extend beyond characterizing the origin of Río Tinto by informing models of acidic rock drainage generation, guiding bioremediation strategies for the simultaneous removal of nitrate and heavy metals from contaminated waters, and providing analogs for potential microbial life in iron-rich, anoxic extraterrestrial environments such as early Mars.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Spatial recovery and persistence of Pseudomonas chlororaphis M71 and Trichoderma atroviride SC1 in grapevine following stem injection.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Establishing biocontrol agents (BCAs) within grapevine tissues could provide a means of protecting internal plant compartments, but little is known about their spatial and temporal fate after vascular delivery or whether the graft union constrains their distribution. We compared the internal recovery of two biologically contrasting BCAs, the bacterium Pseudomonas chlororaphis M71 and the filamentous fungus Trichoderma atroviride SC1, following controlled stem injection into rooted and grafted grapevine plants. A xylem-mobile dye was used as a reference for immediate passive fluid transport, while viable microbial recovery was assessed over time and complemented by quantitative isolation and microscopy. At 48 h, the dye generally showed broader longitudinal distribution than either of the microorganisms. The two microorganisms displayed markedly different patterns. M71 persisted for up to 56 days, but remained predominantly associated with tissues close to the injection site. In contrast, SC1 was recovered from a broader range of tissues, including roots, and remained detectable for up to 56 days. In grafted plants, both microorganisms were recovered on both sides of the graft union, indicating that the graft interface was not an absolute barrier, although recovery depended on microbial identity and inoculation position. Green fluorescent protein-labeled M71 cells and SC1 hyphae were observed within xylem vessels, confirming internal localization and, for SC1, vegetative development after injection. These results show that, and how, both microbial biology and grafted-plant architecture influence the internal fate of injected BCAs in grapevine.IMPORTANCEBeneficial microorganisms established inside grapevine tissues could potentially protect from infections regarding internal tissues, but little is known about how such microorganisms distribute and persist inside grapevine after injection into the plant tissues. This study shows that two biocontrol agents (BCAs) with contrasting biological characteristics follow markedly different spatial and temporal patterns. Pseudomonas chlororaphis M71 persisted mainly near the site of introduction, whereas Trichoderma atroviride SC1 was recovered from a broader range of tissues and developed hyphae within xylem vessels. Importantly, the graft union was not an absolute barrier to microbial recovery. These findings provide a framework for selecting where and when BCAs should be introduced during grapevine propagation and highlight that vascular access, persistence, and broad within-plant establishment are distinct properties that should be considered when developing endophytic biocontrol strategies.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Mechanistic insights into atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP)-induced genomic alterations and phenotypic evolution in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP) is a potent tool for microbial strain engineering; however, the mechanistic basis of its genome-wide mutagenic effects remains poorly understood. Utilizing Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model, we performed a comprehensive characterization of the mutational landscape and DNA repair pathways elicited by ARTP. Under high-lethality conditions (~99% mortality), ARTP treatment induced a substantial mutational burden, with SNVs and InDels rates increasing 25.2- and 36.7-fold relative to untreated controls, respectively. These mutations exhibited a pronounced bias toward C-T/G-A and A-T/T-A substitutions and InDels within AT-rich regions. Remarkably, the frequency of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) surged 57.4-fold, suggesting a potent capacity for inducing DNA breaks. Through sectored colony assays, we demonstrate that ARTP primarily inflicts pre-replicative double-strand breaks (DSBs), with reciprocal crossovers serving as the predominant driver of terminal LOH. The distribution and pattern of LOH were also altered in ARTP-treated cells. Mechanistically, our study establishes that the translesion synthesis polymerases Rev1 and Pol ζ are indispensable for converting ARTP-induced lesions-likely pyrimidine dimers-into fixed point mutations. In contrast, Rad30 facilitates high-fidelity bypass across these dimers. The base excision repair pathway appears largely dispensable for the processing of these lesions. In contrast, the nucleotide excision repair pathway plays a predominant role in mitigating ARTP-induced mutations. Finally, the strategic application of iterative ARTP mutagenesis facilitated the rapid evolution of acetate-tolerant strains. Our findings provide fundamental insights into the molecular signatures of ARTP mutagenesis, offering a framework for its optimized application in directed evolution. [IMPORTANCE] While ARTP is a cornerstone of non-thermal mutagenesis in industrial biotechnology, its genetic impact has long been treated as a "black box." This study provides a high-resolution molecular dissection of ARTP-induced genomic alterations using a diploid yeast model. We demonstrate that ARTP is not merely a source of point mutations but a potent catalyst for pre-replicative double-strand breaks and extensive mitotic recombination. By elucidating the pivotal roles of specific DNA repair pathways in mutation fixation, we transition ARTP from a purely empirical screening tool to a mechanistically grounded platform for directed evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of this platform by evolving acetate-tolerant strains and identifying the underlying genetic drivers of their resilience.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Rapid detection of the oak wilt pathogen (Bretziella fagacearum) using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP).
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Oak wilt, caused by Bretziella fagacearum, is a destructive disease of Quercus species. Symptoms consist of leaf scorch, dieback, defoliation, vascular discoloration, and eventual death. Prompt diagnosis is crucial for timely management that involves laborious and expensive practices such as sanitation, cutting of infected trees, and proactive tree removal to create a buffer zone, root trenching, and/or fungicide injections. Due to these resource-intensive management tactics, laboratory test accuracy and speed are paramount. Diagnoses of oak wilt currently rely on culturing, nested PCR, or qPCR, but all these methods have limitations, ranging from ambiguous results to high barriers to application. We developed a rapid, robust, and sensitive loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) diagnostic test using primers and probes that target a section of the internal transcribed spacer region of the rDNA of the oak wilt pathogen, B. fagacearum. This assay can detect B. fagacearum from pure isolates and environmental samples, including branch sapwood, leaf petioles, nitidulid sap beetle vectors, and degraded fungal mats. The LAMP assay developed here is sensitive to a detection limit as low as 1 pg/μL and can detect the pathogen in under 20 min. This real-time LAMP-based diagnostic test is thoroughly validated to specifically detect the oak wilt pathogen, B. fagacearum, and is demonstrated to detect the fungus from a variety of routinely collected sample types.
