Our rapid molecular detection protocol can provide a useful tool for diagnostic labs, forest health practitioners, and researchers studying oak wilt.IMPORTANCEOak wilt is a deadly disease of oaks that represents a growing threat to natural and planted forests throughout eastern North America. To enhance the speed and accuracy of molecular diagnostics for this disease, we designed a molecular test using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) to reliably and rapidly detect the oak wilt pathogen, Bretziella fagacearum. To optimize the practicality of this assay in real-world conditions, we developed a rigorous validation process that incorporated the known breadth of genetic diversity of the oak wilt pathogen, sample tissue range, and a panel of non-target fungi to assess the potential for false positives. The novel assay is demonstrated to be highly specific and can detect B. fagacearum from host sapwood, leaf petioles, and nitidulid sap beetles, serving as a versatile new tool for forest health surveillance. Our approach also represents a thorough framework for researchers interested in the development of rapid molecular methods for the detection of forest microbes more broadly.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Nest ecology-associated impacts of wastewater on wild bee microbiomes.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Anthropogenic pollution affects environments differently depending on proximity to the pollution source, exposure route, and species ecology. Thus, understanding an organism's ecological role and exposure route to contaminants is central to assessing pollution impact. Treated municipal wastewater releases contaminants into waterways and alters microbial communities. Plants absorb contaminants and expose animals through foraging and nest-building activities. Nesting ecology differences of ground and wood cavity-nesting bees offer insight into niche-specific susceptibility to pollution. We compared gut microbiomes of directly exposed soil-nesting Halictus ligatus and indirectly exposed wood-nesting Ceratina spp. upstream and downstream of wastewater. We collected bees, flowers, and soil and analyzed their bacterial microbiomes using 16S rRNA sequencing. The effect from wastewater explained a much larger proportion of the variance in the ground-nesting H. ligatus microbiome than wood cavity-nesting Ceratina adults, Ceratina larvae, and pollen provisions. Conversely, soil and flower microbiomes remained stable, indicating higher stability. These findings suggest that wastewater exposure leads to strong host-associated microbiome disruption, with ground-nesting bees most affected.IMPORTANCEBecause contaminants bind strongly to soil, ground-nesting bees near wastewater are likely most impacted, while wood cavity-nesting bees are likely less impacted since plant uptake of contaminants is species dependent. These results suggest that exposure routes drive contaminant susceptibility, with bee-associated microbes most vulnerable. Because bees are important pollinators and biodiversity contributors, these disruptions point to broader ecological risks in increasingly contaminated landscapes.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Plasmid-mediated copper resistance in Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans: determination of plasmid copy number and stability.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: The management of bacterial spot of tomato is challenged by the widespread occurrence of copper resistance among its causal pathogens. In Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans, a major causal agent, copper resistance is conferred by cop genes organized in an operon located on either the chromosome or plasmid. In the United States, copper resistance is predominantly chromosomally encoded. Plasmid-borne resistance is limited to a few phylogenetic groups but is prevalent in other bacterial spot pathogens. We hypothesized that plasmid-encoded copper resistance genes exhibit higher expression than chromosomally encoded genes but may be unstable in the absence of selective pressure for resistance. To test this hypothesis, we examined how the chromosomal versus plasmid-borne cop operon influences gene copy number and expression, as well as plasmid stability. Relative to strains with only chromosomal resistance, strains carrying plasmid-encoded resistance exhibited an increased copy number of copB, a key gene in the operon, while strains carrying both chromosomal and plasmid-encoded resistance showed an even greater increase in gene copy number. Correspondingly, copB expression was elevated in both groups. During in vitro growth without copper, partial or complete plasmid loss occurred in a subset of strains, and genome sequencing of colonies with reduced plasmid size revealed transposase-mediated plasmid rearrangements. These findings demonstrate that plasmid-borne copper resistance increases gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes but can be unstable without copper selection in some strain backgrounds, highlighting the role of mobile genetic elements in shaping Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans adaptation to changing copper environments.IMPORTANCEPlasmids are key players in the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance. Although copper resistance is widespread among Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans strains, copper-based bactericides remain at the forefront of disease management. We previously demonstrated that distinct genetic elements, including plasmid- and chromosomally encoded genomic islands, contribute to the acquisition of copper resistance and the occurrence of multicopy resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans. Here, we show that the localization of copper resistance genes on a plasmid, chromosome, or both influences gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes. Furthermore, rearrangements between co-resident plasmids affect plasmid stability, leading to the loss of copper resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans. These findings highlight how plasmid dynamics can shape bacterial evolvability and adaptation to selective environments.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Lineage II Escherichia coli O157:H7: genomes, prophages, colicins, and the absence of detectable Stx2.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: The genomes of three lineage II strains of E. coli O157:H7 (FRIK2069, FRIK2455, and FRIK2533) with different pulsed-field gel electrophoresis patterns were sequenced, assembled, and compared. The genomes were closely related, with overall synteny, with the exception of a 302 kbp inversion in FRIK2069. FRIK2533 lacked pO157, which may account for its limited isolation. FRIK2455 was the dominant strain isolated over several years and was selected for comparison with lineage I (Sakai) and lineage I/II (EC4115) strains. Distinct polymorphisms were identified in prophages and MGEs among the three lineages. All lineages contained stx1 prophages and the locus of enterocyte effacement. The stx2a prophage was present in Sakai and EC4115, while the stx2c prophage was found in EC4115 and FRIK2455. Eleven geographically disparate LII strains from the United States were tested for functional phage and Stx2. Three of the 11 LII strains underwent delayed lysis after 24 h post-mitomycin C treatment. stx2 transcription was observed in two of the three lytic strains, but Stx2 was not detected in the lytic or non-lytic LII strains by Western blot. The supernatant of lysates from eight lineage II strains inhibited growth of the phage host (E. coli strain MG1655) due to the production of a colicin (D, B, or M). These findings add to the body of evidence that LII EHEC do not produce functional phage or a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may be key characteristics to the persistence of EHEC strains in the bovine host and farm environment.IMPORTANCEEscherichia coli O157:H7 is a human pathogen that is phylogenetically separated into three lineages. Strains belonging to lineages I and I/II are isolated from both clinical and bovine samples, whereas lineage II strains are only isolated from bovine and environments they occupy. This study sequenced, assembled, and compared the genomes of three lineage II strains. The genomes were closely related and syntenic, with differences in plasmid content and a chromosomal inversion. Comparison of the genome from FRIK2455 (lineage II strain) with the genomes of lineage I and I/II strains found distinct polymorphisms in prophages and mobile genetic elements. None of the lineage II strains examined produced functional phage or Stx2, but eight strains produced a colicin. Results from this study support previous reports that lineage II strains do not produce a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may contribute to the persistence of EHEC in bovine.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Electron transfer to nitrogenase in Paenibacillus polymyxa.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Nitrogenase requires low-potential electrons to reduce N2 to produce ammonia. The direct electron donors to nitrogenase are reduced ferredoxin (Fd) and flavodoxin (Fld). The enzymes that reduce Fd or Fld for N2 fixation mainly include pyruvate-flavodoxin (ferredoxin) oxidoreductase (PFOR), ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase (FNR), Rhodobacter nitrogen fixation protein complex (Rnf), and bifurcating electron transfer flavoprotein complex (Fix). Paenibacillus polymyxa is a model for studies of nitrogen fixation, but the pathways of electron transport to nitrogenase are unknown. In this study, we characterized the electron transport pathway to nitrogenase in P. polymyxa. Deletion analysis showed that among 15 genes encoding Fds, Fld, and Fd-/Fld-reducing enzymes, only cbiW gene and pfoAB operon decreased nitrogenase activity (31% and 37% relative to wild type, respectively). Triple deletion of cbiW and pfoAB led to a reduction of nitrogenase activity by 61%. Elemental analysis and ultraviolet-visible absorption spectroscopy revealed that the purified Fd protein encoded by cbiW is a [2Fe-2S] Fd. The purified Fd protein was able to substitute for Klebsiella NifF (Fld) to transfer electrons from pyruvate to Klebsiella nitrogenase in vitro. The pfoAB operon encodes PFOR, which is composed of two subunits. Klebsiella oxytoca NifJ (PFOR) was able to support nitrogen fixation in the ΔpfoAB mutant. These findings suggest that [2Fe-2S] Fd encoded by cbiW and PFOR encoded by the pfoAB operon constitute an electron transport pathway to Paenibacillus nitrogenase. [IMPORTANCE] Gram-positive and facultatively anaerobic Paenibacillus polymyxa is a model diazotroph whose nif (nitrogen fixation) genes encoding nitrogenase have been used for engineering yeast and plants. However, the pathway of electron transfer to Paenibacillus nitrogenase is unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that Fd encoded by cbiW and PFOR encoded by the pfoAB operon constitute an electron transport pathway to Paenibacillus nitrogenase. Fd encoded by cbiW is a [2Fe-2S] Fd, and PFOR encoded by the pfoAB operon is a heterodimer. In contrast, in many gram-negative diazotrophs, [4Fe-4S] Fds are widely used as electron donors to nitrogenase, and PFORs (NifJs) are homodimers. These results suggest that there may be some differences in the mechanisms of electron transfer to nitrogenase between gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria. The identified electron transport components in P. polymyxa will have great potential for use in engineering eukaryotes.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Chemical diversity analysis identifies inhibitory compounds in the secretomes of citrus-associated Bacillus spp. to the Huanglongbing pathogen, "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus," and citrus root pathogens.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Huanglongbing (HLB) is a devastating and incurable citrus disease associated with the gram-negative, phloem-limited, and unculturable bacterium "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus" (CLas), transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri. Our goal was to identify high-performing microbial candidates from a previously established citrus-associated microbial collection for the management of HLB and associated root pathogens. Candidate selection was based on bioactivity, genomic, and metabolomic profiles. Eighteen Bacillus isolates were screened for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens, CLas, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the isolates into four species groups: Bacillus velezensis, B. subtilis, B. pumilus, and B. cereus. Among these, B. velezensis exhibited the strongest and broadest inhibitory activity, followed by B. subtilis. This enhanced antagonistic potential is likely associated with the greater number and diversity of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) identified. Notably, CLas-inhibitory isolates included B. velezensis (CB0021 and CB0909) and B. altitudinis (CB0086). Bacilysin and surfactin BGCs were conserved across all CLas-inhibitory isolates, suggesting a potential role in CLas suppression. Accordingly, surfactins were detected in bioactive fractions of B. velezensis (CB0027 and CB0909) and B. subtilis (CB0893), supporting their likely contribution to bioactivity and inhibiting L. crescens growth in vitro, highlighting their potential as candidate compounds for CLas management. Overall, this study underscores the importance of microbial discovery, screening, and characterization as an effective strategy for identifying sustainable solutions to manage HLB.IMPORTANCEHuanglongbing (HLB) is a severe disease of citrus that has altered the citrus landscape worldwide and currently has no cure. It is caused by the bacterium "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus" (CLas) and transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri. Currently, the most effective control strategy for this disease relies on trunk injection of antibiotics oxytetracycline and streptomycin, and there is a need to find alternative solutions to complement or replace chemical control. Here, we aimed to select high-performing candidates from our previously established citrus-associated microbial collection to manage HLB and root-associated pathogens. We screened 18 Bacillus isolates for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens, CLas, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp., and we generated their genomic and metabolomic profiles. Our research centers on selecting microbial candidates for their bioactivity and antimicrobial metabolite production, aiming to develop effective plant-protective bioinoculants for mitigation of HLB.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Wildlife-associated ecosystems in Algeria harbor internationally distributed ESBL-producing clones and plasmids, including a CTX-M-15 Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 lineage associated with a conserved IncFIB(K) resistance plasmid.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) have disseminated beyond clinical settings, but their occurrence and genomic epidemiology in wildlife remain poorly characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. ESC-R may result from the production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) or AmpC-type cephalosporinases. We investigated the prevalence, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-R-E in free-ranging wildlife, captive wild animals, and zoo workers in Algeria. Between October 2021 and June 2023, 1,899 fecal samples were collected across six Algerian provinces. ESC-R-E isolates were recovered by selective culture and characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. Overall, 73 ESC-R-E isolates (3.9%) were identified, including seven OXA-48-like carbapenemase co-producers (0.4%). Carriage was significantly higher in captive animals (13.5%) than in free-ranging wildlife (1.6%) or zoo workers (7.7%). Among the 66 ESBL-producing isolates analyzed, CTX-M enzymes predominated (n = 61), particularly CTX-M-15 (n = 53). Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant species (n = 33), with ST17 accounting for 27/33 isolates. Closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST17 isolates were recovered from captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and a zoo worker and carried an IncFIB(K) plasmid harboring blaCTX-M-15 within a multidrug resistance region closely related to globally disseminated plasmids. Globally disseminated high-risk Escherichia coli clones were also detected, namely ST167, ST361, ST410, and a persistent ST38 lineage in Algerian wildlife since 2016. These findings demonstrate the circulation of high-risk Enterobacterales lineages and mobile resistance plasmids in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems and highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance at the human-animal-environment interface. [IMPORTANCE] Wildlife is increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir and sentinel for antimicrobial resistance, yet genomic data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce. This study provides one of the largest genomic investigations of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife from North Africa. We demonstrate that internationally disseminated high-risk Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli lineages, together with globally distributed CTX-M-15-carrying plasmids, are circulating among captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and humans in zoological environments. The recovery of closely related K. pneumoniae ST17 isolates from different host species highlights the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination across the human-animal-environment interface. These findings extend the known ecological range of clinically important resistant Enterobacterales beyond healthcare settings and identify wildlife-associated ecosystems as part of the broader antimicrobial resistance network. Our study underscores the value of integrating wildlife into One Health surveillance programs to better understand and mitigate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Antidepressant desvenlafaxine identified in wastewater promotes transformation and antibiotic resistance risk in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 via metabolic adaptations.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are known reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Non-antibiotic compounds, such as antidepressants, may further promote ARG acquisition through horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Desvenlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) listed on the EU Surface Water Watch List, is among the most frequently detected antidepressants in WWTP effluents, yet its role in HGT has not been examined. Here, we detected desvenlafaxine at the highest concentrations among four antidepressants monitored across three municipal WWTPs in western New York. Using Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 as a model recipient in natural transformation assays (n = 6), we found that desvenlafaxine significantly increased transformation frequency at 10 mg/L (1.74 ± 0.33-fold) and 50 mg/L (1.49 ± 0.19-fold; Padj < 0.05). Effects occurred without induction of reactive oxygen species or loss of membrane integrity, consistent with its very low toxicity (IC20 ~1,300 mg/L). Instead, desvenlafaxine induced dose-dependent increases in membrane fluidity and shifts to less negative zeta potentials, suggesting that electrostatic interactions between its cationic amine group and the negatively charged membrane reduce surface repulsion and facilitate plasmid proximity during uptake. Non-targeted proteomics revealed a biphasic response: at 10 mg/L, competence-associated proteins (PilB, ComM) were upregulated, and STRING analysis identified networks linked to membrane transport, transcriptional regulation, and envelope remodeling, while no connected network was recovered at 50 mg/L. Electron microscopy confirmed higher pilus frequency at both doses. Together, these findings reveal a non-oxidative, envelope-mediated route by which a widely detected antidepressant increases bacterial competence.IMPORTANCEThe spread of antibiotic resistance poses a serious and escalating threat to human health worldwide. While antibiotic use is widely recognized as a key driver, non-antibiotic pharmaceuticals released into the environment through wastewater have received far less attention. Antidepressants are among the most frequently detected drugs in treated wastewater effluents, yet their potential to promote antibiotic resistance transfer in bacteria remains poorly understood. This study demonstrates that desvenlafaxine, one of the most abundant antidepressants found in municipal wastewater, can increase the uptake of antibiotic resistance genes in an environmental bacterium at concentrations above those currently measured in effluent, and identifies the bacterial cell-surface changes that enable this without cytotoxicity.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Local temperature and humidity are associated with proportion of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli isolates in farm environments: considerations for on-farm surveillance.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Evidence suggests that increased local temperatures are associated with higher prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental bacteria. This observational cohort study investigates associations between local climate and the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli isolated from 2,766 farm environment samples from 53 English dairy farms. A non-linear Bayesian model that accounts for decreased test sensitivity at low E. coli abundance was used to estimate the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli from colony count data. A 20°C increase in local temperature was associated with a 5.0-fold increase in the proportion of streptomycin-resistant E. coli (95% credible interval [CI]: 1.03-33.0; absolute increase: 0.2%, 95% CI: 2.3 × 10-3%-1.2%). Weaker evidence suggested that increased temperatures were associated with increased proportions of tetracycline-resistant E. coli. Increasing relative humidity was associated with an increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-, streptomycin-, and tetracycline-resistant E. coli. A 32% increase in relative humidity (from 60% to 92%) was associated with a 4.7-fold increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-resistant E. coli (median; 95% CI: 1.4-15.7; absolute increase: 1.3%, 95% CI: 0.2%-3.5%). For amoxicillin and streptomycin, a synergistic effect where increasing both temperature and humidity was associated with increased proportions of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli was observed, with weak evidence of this effect observed for tetracycline. These findings highlight the importance of considering weather conditions, sample characteristics, and seasonality in livestock AMR surveillance. Associations between local weather conditions and the proportion of livestock E. coli exhibiting AMR suggest that climate change may influence the burden of One Health AMR.IMPORTANCEUnderstanding how environmental conditions are associated with variability in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence is critical for developing robust livestock AMR surveillance and anticipating the potential effects of climate change. The non-linear Bayesian modeling approach developed here adjusts for Escherichia coli abundance-associated variability in test sensitivity, enabling the influence of risk factors associated with the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli within samples to be more accurately estimated. Applying this approach to 2,766 fecal samples from 53 dairy farms in Southwest England indicated that the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli generally increased under warmer and wetter conditions. These findings suggest that environmental conditions can influence the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli in dairy farm environments and demonstrate the importance of accounting for weather-related variability in livestock AMR surveillance. Adjusting for these associations in livestock AMR surveillance could improve the accuracy of modeling AMR trends and strengthen the assessment of climate-associated AMR risks.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Whole-genome analysis uncovers four novel Streptomyces species linked to sweet potato soil rot in China.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Sweet potato soil rot, caused by pathogenic Streptomyces, is an emerging threat to sweet potato production in China. However, the diversity and pathogenic mechanisms of the associated species remain poorly understood. In this study, symptomatic storage roots exhibiting typical pox-like lesions were collected from major production regions in Henan and Guangdong provinces. A total of 225 actinomycete strains were isolated using optimized methods, and six highly pathogenic strains were identified through tuber slice, hydroponic, and pot inoculation assays. Morphological, physiological, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analyses revealed considerable diversity among these pathogenic isolates. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) analysis showed that strain (ST10) was closely related to Streptomyces albogriseolus, whereas the remaining strains displayed substantial genomic divergence, indicating diverse taxonomic affiliations. Comparative genomic analysis identified a conserved core genome together with extensive strain-specific gene content, reflecting both functional conservation and adaptive evolution. Phylogenomic analysis placed several isolates close to S. ipomoeae, and others within distinct pathogenic lineages. Notably, none of the six strains possessed the canonical thaxtomin biosynthetic gene cluster, suggesting that pathogenicity is mediated by alternative virulence mechanisms. Instead, conserved gene clusters associated with siderophores and stress-related metabolites were identified, indicating potential roles in host colonization and ecological adaptation. These findings expand our understanding of the genomic diversity and potential pathogenic mechanisms of sweet potato-associated Streptomyces and provide a valuable foundation for disease management and resistance breeding. [IMPORTANCE] Herein, we established an optimized isolation method yielding 225 actinomycete strains and a rapid pipeline for pathogenic identification of sweet potato-associated Streptomyces. Six isolates were confirmed as causal agents of sweet potato soil rot, including four novel species. Complete genome sequences of five strains provide a fundamental resource for elucidating pathogenesis mechanisms and advancing taxonomic and evolutionary studies of the genus. The absence of canonical thaxtomin biosynthetic genes across all pathogenic strains, combined with the presence of conserved siderophore and stress-related metabolite clusters, demonstrates that these pathogens utilize alternative virulence mechanisms distinct from well-characterized Streptomyces plant pathogens. Comparative genomics reveals a conserved core genome alongside strain-specific gene content, reflecting functional conservation and adaptive evolution. These genomic resources and experimental validations establish a foundational framework for understanding pathogen diversity, enabling accurate diagnosis of emerging strains and directly informing resistance breeding programs by identifying genetic targets for screening sweet potato germplasm.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Structural and catalytic characterization of the 2,5-dihydroxypyridine ring-cleaving dioxygenase Hpo from Pseudomonas putida S16.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: 2,5-Dihydroxypyridine (2,5-DHP) is a potentially carcinogenic intermediate in pyridine catabolism. Hpo, a non-heme Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase from Pseudomonas putida S16, catalyzes ring cleavage of 2,5-DHP, yet its structure has remained uncharacterized. We determined the crystal structure of Hpo at 2.56 Å resolution, revealing a catalytic Fe center coordinated by His257, His310, and Asp312 in a conserved 2-His-1-carboxylate motif, with Ser294 positioned directly below the iron and essential for iron binding. The substrate-binding pocket, formed primarily by Phe94, Phe97, Phe186, Phe188, and Arg285, incorporates potential hydrogen-bonding interactions from Glu169 and His181. Hpo employs a distinctive Phe94-Leu95-Leu96-Phe97 motif for substrate recognition, contrasting with the Met102-Leu103-Leu104-His105 motif in the isoenzyme NicX. Molecular dynamics simulations spanning 200 ns demonstrated that Phe94 and Phe97 mutations destabilized substrate binding, confirming their role in substrate recognition, and explaining the corresponding loss of catalytic activity. These findings reveal the active-site architecture and substrate engagement mechanism of Hpo, advancing our understanding of pyridine ring-cleaving non-heme Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenases.IMPORTANCEPyridine compounds are common environmental contaminants that pose risks to human health. The microbial degradation of pyridine compounds generates toxic intermediates, including 2,5-dihydroxypyridine (2,5-DHP), which require enzymatic detoxification. Prior to this study, only one 2,5-DHP dioxygenase had been structurally characterized, leaving the structural basis of this rare enzyme subgroup unresolved. By determining the Hpo crystal structure and identifying residues critical for iron coordination and catalysis, this work addresses a significant knowledge gap and establishes a structural framework for understanding pyridine ring-cleaving non-heme Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenases and may also provide an enzymatic perspective on the removal of pyridine contaminants from the environment.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: N(₂)O reduction at low pH.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Microbial N₂O reduction in acid soils became a conundrum when NosZ maturation was found to be impaired at pH ≤6 in both model organisms and soil communities. Yet, evolution appears to have repeatedly circumvented this constraint. Examples include the identification of two small proteins that enable maturation of canonical NosZ at low pH, as well as the Schinkia sp. isolated by G. He, M. E. Davin, S. Kolodney, E. Stutzman, et al. (Appl Environ Microbiol 92:e00069-26, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.00069-26), which carries a unique repertoire of nosZ genes and grows by N2O respiration across pH 4.4-8.5. These discoveries help resolve the conundrum and may provide new options for mitigating N2O emissions.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Phosphonate degradation through the C-P lyase pathway by a dinoflagellate-associated Mameliella alba enhances host growth under phosphate limitation.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Phosphonates are distinguished by their chemically stable carbon-phosphorus (C-P) bonds and constitute approximately 25% of the dissolved organic P pool in the ocean. Most eukaryotic phytoplankton, including dinoflagellates, are unable to directly utilize extracellular phosphonates. However, their associated bacteria can facilitate indirect exploitation of this P source. This study presents the isolation and characterization of strain DH-1, a dinoflagellate-associated bacterium capable of phosphonate degradation. DH-1 was identified as Mameliella alba, and its genome contains a complete C-P lyase gene cluster. Growth assays demonstrated that DH-1 could maintain growth under conditions with 2-aminoethylphosphonate (2-AEP) as the sole P source, indicating that it can utilize this biogenic phosphonate. RT-qPCR analyses revealed that transcription levels of the C-P lyase subunits phnJ and phnH, as well as the phosphonate transport genes phnC and phnD, were significantly upregulated under phosphate-limited conditions. Furthermore, the expression of phnJ and phnH was also induced by 2-AEP, indicating that C-P lyase pathway in DH-1 is co-regulated by the Pho regulon and substrate induction. The growth of the dinoflagellate Prorocentrum donghaiense was significantly enhanced when both DH-1 and 2-AEP were added to P-limited cultures, whereas the alga did not grow in the presence of either 2-AEP or DH-1 alone. This study presents the first example of a specific dinoflagellate-associated bacterium that can promote algal growth by degrading phosphonates to release phosphate. These interactions are vital for the ecological success of dinoflagellates that live in P-limited environments, offering novel insights into the formation and dynamics of harmful algal blooms.IMPORTANCEPhosphonates are an important component of dissolved organic phosphorus in the ocean. They can serve as a potential phosphorus source when phosphate, which is directly bioavailable to phytoplankton, is scarce in marine environments. While eukaryotic phytoplankton typically lack the capacity to utilize phosphonates, certain algal-associated bacteria possess the ability to degrade these compounds. However, no specific strains have been thoroughly examined. Here, we report the discovery of a bacterial strain capable of phosphonate utilization through a specific metabolic pathway. This bacterium was isolated from the dinoflagellate Prorocentrum donghaiense, one of the most prevalent red tide-forming species in China. It can promote the growth of P. donghaiense by supplying phosphate derived from phosphonate degradation. These findings highlight the critical role of bacteria in facilitating phosphonate utilization by dinoflagellates. This mechanism may contribute to the development of harmful algal blooms, which underscores the ecological importance of the algae-bacteria interactions in marine ecosystems.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Waste oil substrates reshape the black soldier fly larval gut microbiome and biomass composition during bioconversion.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) are generalist decomposers with promise for converting agricultural and food-processing by-products into value-added bioproducts, but BSFL performance on lipid-rich waste oil streams and the role of the gut microbiome in this process remain unclear. Here, we evaluated BSFL bioconversion of a standard chicken feed diet supplemented with three chemically distinct waste oils: acidulated vegetable oil (AVO), pork grease (PG), and used cooking oil (UCO). Larval performance, bioconversion rate, gut microbiome composition, total protein and fat content, and fatty-acid profiles were measured across bioconversion. Larval age was a major driver of gut microbiome structure, but waste oil supplementation further reshaped community membership and structure, with the strongest diet-associated effects occurring during early-to-intermediate bioconversion. Most differentially abundant taxa were members of the baseline core gut community, suggesting that oil supplementation primarily altered dominance patterns among resident taxa. PG and UCO supported larval growth, and bioconversion performance did not differ significantly from the chicken feed control, whereas AVO reduced bioconversion rate and showed weaker growth outcomes. Oil supplementation also increased larval fat content, reduced protein content, and shifted fatty-acid profiles toward the corresponding oil feedstocks, although larval biomass composition remained shaped by basal diet and host or microbial metabolism. These findings suggest that selected lipid-rich waste streams can support efficient BSFL bioconversion while restructuring resident gut microbiome members that may tolerate, metabolize, or indirectly respond to oil-associated conditions, contributing to substrate-dependent changes in larval lipid accumulation and fatty-acid composition. [IMPORTANCE] Agricultural and food-processing systems generate large amounts of lipid-rich by-products that are difficult to manage using conventional waste-valorization approaches. Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) offer a biological route for recovering nutrients from these materials, but efficient conversion depends on interactions among substrate chemistry, larval physiology, and the gut microbiome. This study suggests that some waste oil streams can support larval growth while restructuring resident gut microbial communities and altering larval fatty-acid composition. These findings are important for agricultural biotechnology because they frame BSFL production as a host-microbiome bioconversion system rather than simply an insect-based waste-reduction process. Understanding how gut microbes respond to chemically distinct lipid wastes can guide substrate selection, pretreatment, and microbiome-informed optimization strategies for converting underutilized agricultural and food-processing residues into value-added bioproducts for circular agricultural systems.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: A high-throughput pipeline for isolation and screening of the citrus bacteriome identifies Pseudomonas chlororaphis with anti-Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus activity.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Plant microbiomes are a rich source of secondary metabolites, often with pathogen- or disease-suppressive traits. Huanglongbing (HLB) is a serious disease of citrus for which there is currently no cure. Here, we tested the hypothesis that bacteria native to the citrus microbiome may possess inhibitory activity against the associated causal agent of HLB, Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas). We coupled a robotic microfluidic isolation platform with a high-throughput antimicrobial screening assay using Liberibacter crescens, a culturable surrogate for the unculturable CLas, to identify isolates with anti-Liberibacter activity. We identified 35 bacterial isolates with activity using this pipeline. One strongly inhibitory citrus root isolate, Pseudomonas chlororaphis (SRAM11), was selected for bioassay-guided fractionation. We determined a significant driver of in vitro Liberibacter inhibition was attributed to the production of phenazine-1-carboxamide (PCN) by P. chlororaphis. We also demonstrated significant anti-CLas activity of PCN, comparable to that of oxytetracycline, using an ex vivo citrus hairy root assay. P. chlororaphis and phenazines have been implicated in successful biocontrol of other diseases and represent a new tool with possible application to HLB mitigation.IMPORTANCEHuanglongbing (HLB) is a devastating citrus disease that causes millions of dollars in crop loss each year in the United States alone. In this study, we mined the citrus microbiome for bacteria that produce antimicrobials with suppressive activity against Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, the causal agent of HLB. We demonstrated that the citrus microbiome is a rich source of microorganisms that inhibit Liberibacter spp. We selected a Pseudomonas chlororaphis strain for further characterization and assigned anti-Liberibacter activity to the production of phenazine-1-carboxamide. Phenazine-producing P. chlororaphis strains are known biocontrols in other pathosystems, and this study highlights their potential for mitigation of HLB.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Dinoflagellate blooms reshape bacterioplankton assembly and alter free-living and particle-attached community dynamics with implications for harmful algal bloom processes.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Although shifts in bacterial communities during harmful algal blooms (HABs) have been studied extensively, the assembly processes of bacterioplankton communities across complete bloom cycles remain insufficiently resolved. In this study, based on 16S rRNA gene high-throughput sequencing, we characterized the succession and assembly of bacterioplankton communities across four stages of a coastal bloom caused by Scrippsiella acuminata. We found that the alpha diversity of free-living (FL) bacterioplankton decreased with bloom progression, whereas the alpha diversity of particle-attached (PA) bacterioplankton increased during bloom development. Among taxa that responded strongly to the bloom, Rhodobacteraceae, Flavobacteriaceae, and SAR86_clade showed marked changes in abundance. Null-model analysis suggests that stochastic processes, mainly drift and dispersal limitation, dominated the assembly of both FL and PA bacterial communities, but that the bloom increased the influence of deterministic processes, especially selection. Rhodobacteraceae showed the closest association with the bloom-forming dinoflagellate and may participate in infochemical exchange through compounds such as indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). Together, these results show that bloom progression restructures FL and PA bacterioplankton differently while shifting community assembly toward stronger environmental filtering.IMPORTANCEHarmful algal blooms (HABs) reshape microbial food webs and biogeochemical cycling in coastal waters. This study shows that free-living and particle-attached bacterioplankton respond differently to bloom progression, with contrasting diversity trajectories and distinct taxonomic shifts. It also demonstrates that stochastic assembly remains dominant throughout the bloom, whereas deterministic selection becomes more important during bloom stages. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how HABs restructure marine bacterioplankton and identify bacterial groups potentially involved in bloom-associated interactions.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Cross-domain microbiome legacy of a natural Phaeocystis globosa bloom in eutrophic coastal waters: a framework for monitoring bloom onset, collapse, and post-bloom recovery.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: When a harmful algal bloom collapses, does the coastal water quality recover? We addressed this question using the natural bloom of the haptophyte Phaeocystis globosa in coastal waters around Xiamen Island, China. Bacterial and microeukaryotic communities in the water samples (n = 105) monthly collected from five sites from September 2023 to March 2024 were analyzed using 16S and 18S rRNA amplicon sequencing, genotype-specific qPCR, iCAMP-based assembly inference, partial least squares path modeling, bloom stage-specific co-occurrence networks, and amplicon-based functional prediction. Bloom development drove coordinated physicochemical change. Both bacterial and microeukaryotic communities were displaced from their pre-bloom state but did not return to the original state within the 7-month series. However, their patterns of succession were different. Bacterial communities underwent coherent system-wide succession. They diverged spatially during the bloom. Their assembly shifted toward stochasticity, with the deterministic contribution falling from 46.3% pre-bloom to 27.8% during the bloom and recovering only to 30.3% post-bloom. Their co-occurrence network was most complex during the bloom period. In contrast, microeukaryotic communities retained stronger site-specific structure throughout succession, and their network connectivity peaked after the bloom collapsed. Water quality variables explained 45.9% of bacterial but only 13.1% of microeukaryotic community variation. Predicted functional profiles also showed stage-associated changes. The same bloom thus pushed bacterial and microeukaryotic communities toward different post-disturbance configurations on different timescales. We therefore propose a cross-domain monitoring framework that integrates stage-specific taxa, a community state index, and network complexity. This framework can diagnose bloom onset, collapse, and genuine post-bloom recovery in eutrophic coastal waters.IMPORTANCEHarmful algal blooms disturb coastal waters well beyond the period when the causative alga is abundant. This study shows that the effects of a Phaeocystis globosa bloom on the coastal microbiome lasted after the bloom itself ended and that bacteria and microeukaryotes recovered along different paths and on different timescales. Algal counts or nutrient concentrations alone therefore cannot adequately capture the recovery of coastal water quality. We suggest an alternative monitoring framework that combines stage-specific indicator taxa, a community state index, and network topology, so that coastal water quality can be assessed more reliably.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Design of ancestral protein-glutaminase with improved thermal stability.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Protein-glutaminase (PG) from Chryseobacterium proteolyticum is an industrially valuable enzyme for protein deamidation; however, its application is limited because of insufficient thermal stability. Previous rational design studies have enhanced the thermostability of PG but often required labor-intensive, stepwise optimization. In this study, ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) was used to engineer thermostable PG variants in a single design step. Eight ancestral PGs were constructed, all of which exhibited enhanced thermal stability compared with that of the wild type. The most stable variant, AncPG1, had a melting temperature of 76.2°C, 13.6°C higher than that of the wild type. Mutational dissection identified five substitutions, N148G, N154D, L156Y, L168S, and D179S, that individually enhanced thermal stability and showed cumulative stabilizing effects when combined. These substitutions were predominantly located in surface-associated loop regions. Notably, although the ancestral variants showed reduced catalytic efficiency toward the small synthetic substrate Cbz-Gln-Gly, they retained reactivity toward macromolecular protein substrates when compared at equal activity units. Furthermore, AncPG1 showed greater absolute protein-substrate reactivity than WT CpPG under elevated temperature conditions. These findings provide further support for ASR as a strategy for generating thermostable enzyme variants with improved functional performance under elevated-temperature conditions.IMPORTANCEProtein-glutaminase from Chryseobacterium proteolyticum is used to improve functional properties of food proteins, but its thermal stability limits its use at elevated temperatures. In this study, ancestral sequence reconstruction generated PG variants with substantially increased melting temperatures while retaining reactivity toward protein substrates. AncPG1 also showed greater absolute reactivity than WT CpPG toward multiple protein substrates at 70°C when compared at the same protein concentration. Several substitutions that individually enhanced thermal stability were located in surface-associated loop regions. These results illustrate the utility of evolutionary sequence information for engineering thermostable protein-modifying enzymes.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Assembly mechanisms and successional patterns of sediment bacterial communities along a riverine wetland restoration chronosequence.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Understanding the assembly mechanisms of bacterial communities in sediment is vital for assessing ecological outcomes of wetland restoration. This study examined these processes within sediment bacterial communities along a restoration chronosequence (2, 4, and 8 years) in riverine wetlands. Employing multi-seasonal sampling combined with 16S rRNA gene sequencing, null model frameworks, and co-occurrence network analyses, we observed distinct stage-dependent differences in community assembly. The 2-year wetland was characterized by a relatively high contribution of stochastic processes (notably dispersal limitation), although deterministic processes already dominated assembly. With increasing restoration age, the influence of deterministic processes, especially homogeneous selection, strengthened and remained dominant through the late stage (8 years). Community assembly exhibited significant spatiotemporal variation, with seasonal fluctuations strongly associated with this variation. Concurrently, bacterial co-occurrence networks demonstrated increased modularity, indicative of increasingly modular, functionally compartmentalized community structures. Network topology differed consistently along the restoration gradient, from simple and loosely connected to highly complex and modular configurations, reflecting ecosystem maturation. These findings reveal a pattern of increasing deterministic selection and network modularity with restoration age, thereby advancing understanding of microbial processes during wetland restoration and providing a scientific foundation for ecosystem recovery assessment.IMPORTANCEWetland restoration is widely regarded as a nature-based solution, yet the microbial recovery trajectories following restoration remain poorly characterized. Our study reveals a consistent pattern across restoration ages in sediment bacterial communities across 2-, 4-, and 8-year restored wetlands: from relatively high stochasticity alongside dominant deterministic selection, to strengthened deterministic dominance, and finally to modular, functionally compartmentalized networks. This pattern is associated with restoration duration itself, not with measured environmental factors, and occurs despite strong seasonal variation. Importantly, we show that co-occurrence network modularity and robustness can serve as quantitative, sensitive indicators of ecosystem maturation-more informative than traditional diversity indices. These findings provide a scientific basis for evaluating restoration success and suggest that allowing at least 8 years is necessary for functional stabilization. Our work offers microbial ecological criteria to guide adaptive management and engineering decisions in nature-based wetland restoration.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Aggregation and toxicity in bacteria of Rep-WH1 prion-like proteins from the phytopathogen Xylella fastidiosa.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Xylella fastidiosa is a global bacterial phytopathogen that colonizes the xylem vessels, leading to their occlusion and thus to plant death. The expression of the amyloidogenic, prion-like WH1 domain of the replication protein RepA from the Pseudomonas savastanoi plasmid pPS10 severely damages Escherichia coli cells. Here, we characterize the WH1 domains in the Rep proteins from the X. fastidiosa plasmids pXF51 and pXF64. The expression of these Rep-WH1 proteins, as happens with the archetypical RepA-WH1 protein from pPS10, decreased the culturability of E. coli in vitro, promoting dormancy. Expression of pXF51 Rep-WH1 causes the conversion of the bacillary cells into large cocci in which this protein forms a hydrogel, whereas pXF64 Rep-WH1 generates compact amyloid-like aggregates, as do those for pPS10 RepA-WH1, thus defining distinct protein-specific phase separations. In X. fastidiosa, the Rep-WH1 proteins also reduce culturability by altering the integrity of the cell envelope, driving bacterial cells into dormancy, while co-aggregation of a subset of the X. fastidiosa host proteins probably contribute to reducing bacterial virulence in plants. These findings open a way to the exploitation of the intrinsic amyloidogenic potential of endogenous plasmid-encoded Rep proteins for the control of X. fastidiosa, aiming to reduce its economic and environmental impact.IMPORTANCEXylella fastidiosa is a bacterial pathogen that causes the withering of many woody plants. Currently, there is no efficient way to eradicate this phytopathogen, which menaces crops and natural environments worldwide. In this study, we show that the expression in X. fastidiosa and E. coli of Rep-WH1 proteins, originally encoded by plasmids found either in X. fastidiosa or in Pseudomonas, leads to their aggregation as prions (i.e., transmissible protein particles) that impact bacterial cells by significantly reducing their fitness and, potentially, their virulence. These findings on prion-like Rep-WH1 proteins may constitute the grounds for the development of an efficient weapon against X. fastidiosa.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Epigenetics as a design variable in heterologous expression.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Heterologous expression-the expression of genes from one organism into another-is an important approach to produce value-added chemicals such as proteins and metabolites. The main challenge, however, is achieving high production yields that are commercially viable. Approaches used to improve productivity rely on editing the DNA sequence, including promoters, ribosome binding sites, and codon usage. Epigenetics, in the form of DNA methylation, may offer an additional layer of control to improve production yields but remains unexplored. Moreover, the choice of the host organism is crucial. We have been interested in developing the alternative bacterial host Burkholderia sp. FERM BP-3421. Four DNA methyltransferases were predicted to be encoded in the genome of this strain, one of which was silent under our growth conditions. After performing gene deletions or overexpression, we experimentally assigned the recognition motif of each DNA methyltransferase, one of which was shown to be essential. As expected, modulation of DNA methylation had major impacts on the transcriptome and metabolome of the host, varying depending on which DNA methyltransferase was modified. Two of the methyltransferases that methylate adenine had overlapping profiles, whereas the one methylating cytosine differed. Finally, we probed the role of DNA methylation during heterologous expression using green fluorescence protein and three different promoters. Expression levels varied in a context-dependent manner with mechanisms, in some cases, involving the presence of methylation motifs within promoter regions but also based on global host effects. This work establishes epigenetics as an important design variable to help improve heterologous expression yields.IMPORTANCEImproving heterologous expression currently relies on modifying the DNA sequence. Epigenetics offers an opportunity to improve outcomes but remains unexplored. We first investigated the effect of epigenetic DNA methylation on the growth, transcriptome, and metabolome of an alternative bacterial host we are interested in developing by generating three single, DNA methyltransferase mutants. Next, we showed that epigenetic DNA methylation or the lack thereof can affect heterologous expression outcomes. The effect was context-dependent, reaching 2.4-fold improvement in one instance. This work highlights the importance of being epigenetics-aware during host development for heterologous expression.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Cobamide-based interactions between soil bacteria can be predicted based on monoculture growth.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Interactions between microbes shape the structure and function of microbial communities. While studying interactions is key to understanding microbial communities as a whole, gaining a detailed mechanistic view is challenging due to the number of co-occurring interactions. Here, we focus on a single class of shared nutrients, the cobalamin (vitamin B12) family of enzyme cofactors known as cobamides, to study nutrient interactions in laboratory consortia of increasing complexity. Measuring cobamide-dependent growth of two soil Caulobacter isolates in monoculture revealed that each grows faster within a distinct range of cobamide concentrations. Co-culturing the two isolates demonstrated that the cobamide concentration predictably determines which isolate predominates. These results suggest that, although the two organisms appear functionally redundant, with identical metabolic capabilities predicted in their genomes, they may occupy distinct niches in their environment based on cobamide concentration. We further examined the ability of cobamide-producing Mesorhizobium and Priestia isolates to share cobamides and found that both support the cobamide-dependent growth of the two Caulobacter isolates. The Caulobacter isolates could coexist in tri-cultures with each producer following serial passaging, indicating the producers can support the growth of multiple cobamide-dependent organisms. We analyzed the metabolic capacity encoded in the genomes of the four isolates and found that cobamides are likely the main shared nutrient in our co- and tri-cultures. These results highlight the utility of cobamides as a model nutrient to characterize and predict interactions in bacterial consortia of increasing complexity.IMPORTANCEInteractions between microbes shape their communities and the world around them. Because microbial communities are physically and chemically complex, predicting microbial interactions is often difficult. Using a set of four bacteria isolated from the same soil environment, we generated and tested predictions about the interactions involving a family of model nutrients related to cobalamin (vitamin B12). Understanding and predicting interactions can lead to greater insights into microbiome function.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Nitrate potentiates kanamycin activity in bacteria through metabolic reprogramming and CpxR-associated respiratory activation.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Antibiotic resistance in foodborne bacteria profoundly compromises the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies and represents a persistent global threat to public health and livestock production. There is therefore an urgent need to develop adjuvant strategies that can improve the activity of existing antibiotics against drug-resistant pathogens. In this study, comparative proteomic profiling of kanamycin-susceptible and laboratory-passaged kanamycin-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis (S. Enteritidis) revealed coordinated differences in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, nitrogen metabolism, and the respiratory electron transport chain. The resistant strain displayed reduced NADH production, proton motive force (PMF), and intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Because these proteomic analyses were performed under antibiotic-free conditions and whole-genome sequencing was not conducted, these differences are interpreted as physiological features associated with the resistant phenotype rather than as evidence of the specific genetic mechanism responsible for the increased kanamycin MIC. Mechanistically, nitrate acted as a potent kanamycin adjuvant by increasing cellular bioenergetic activity through the nitrate-glutamine-glutamate-associated pathway. Nitrate increased NADH production, enhanced TCA cycle activity, and elevated PMF, thereby increasing intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Nitrate also altered CpxR-associated regulation of respiratory genes, providing an additional route by which respiratory activity could be enhanced. Genetic disruption of nitrate transport or selected metabolic and regulatory components attenuated nitrate-mediated potentiation, supporting contributions from both metabolic flux and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation. Importantly, nitrate enhanced kanamycin-mediated killing not only in the laboratory-derived Kana-R strain but also in kanamycin-susceptible Kana-S, indicating a general kanamycin-potentiating effect rather than specific reversal of an acquired resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved treatment outcomes against clinically resistant S. Enteritidis isolates, including increased survival in murine and chicken infection models. Collectively, these findings identify nitrate as a metabolic adjuvant that can potentiate kanamycin activity by increasing bacterial bioenergetics and drug accumulation. They further illustrate how bacterial physiological state can modulate aminoglycoside efficacy without establishing that nitrate reverses the underlying genetic mechanism of kanamycin resistance.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic efficacy is influenced not only by inherited resistance determinants but also by the physiological and metabolic state of bacterial cells. Our study shows that nitrate can potentiate kanamycin activity in Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis by enhancing central metabolism, respiratory activity, proton motive force, and intracellular drug accumulation. This potentiation was observed in both a kanamycin-resistant laboratory-passaged strain and a kanamycin-susceptible strain, supporting a general adjuvant effect rather than specific reversal of a defined resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved outcomes in animal infection models using resistant strains. These findings identify inorganic nitrogen metabolism and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation as potential leverage points for developing aminoglycoside adjuvant strategies.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Multiple factors contribute to guaiacol production by Alicyclobacillus acidoterrestris and Alicyclobacillus suci in apple juice, as revealed by transcriptomic and phenotypic analyses.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Alicyclobacillus acidoterrestris and Alicyclobacillus suci are guaiacol-producing bacteria that can spoil fruit juices. To study the genetic underpinnings of guaiacol production in juice, transcriptomics was performed on multiple strains of A. suci and A. acidoterrestris under guaiacol production conditions. While guaiacol production was consistently higher by A. acidoterrestris than by A. suci, the gene expression levels associated with guaiacol production (e.g., vdcC, vdcB, vdcD) showed significant variability across strains of both species, suggesting that other factors beyond vdcC transcription influence the amount of guaiacol produced. A. acidoterrestris exhibited a maximum growth rate at 40°C, but produced the most guaiacol at 25°C (16.2 ± 0.6 µg/L, day 14), suggesting that guaiacol is not only linked to growth. When adjusting pH, A. acidoterrestris produced the most guaiacol at pH 4.0 at 14 days (3.2 ± 2.2 µg/L). A. suci also showed the highest amount of guaiacol production at 25°C (3.6 ± 0.3 µg/L, day 7). In pH-adjusted apple juice, A. suci showed consistent growth across all pH levels, yet produced the most guaiacol at pH 3.0 (2.1 ± 0.08 µg/L, day 7). Importantly, guaiacol levels did not consistently correlate with bacterial growth, underscoring the limitations of enumeration-based spoilage assessments. Comparative strain analysis revealed species-specific differences, with A. acidoterrestris producing significantly more guaiacol in apple juice than A. suci, a trend not reflected in media-based PECA assays. These findings highlight the need to evaluate spoilage risk in relevant food matrices under realistic storage conditions to provide beverage producers with insights for improved mitigation strategies. [IMPORTANCE] Beverage spoilage caused by microbes such as Alicyclobacillus poses a significant challenge for the food industry, leading to substantial economic losses and increased food waste. While it is known that some species, specifically those that produce the off-flavor compound guaiacol, are responsible for spoilage, current risk assessment practices often fail to accurately predict spoilage potential. These practices are often flawed because they rely on simple bacterial enumeration or use media-based assays without relevance to a specific food matrix, which do not reflect real-world conditions. Testing the presence or absence of these bacteria without assessment of spoilage can lead to false positives and overly conservative product disposition decisions. This study highlights the need for a more nuanced approach by demonstrating that the relationship between bacterial growth, gene expression, and guaiacol production is not straightforward as it impacts juice spoilage.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Deep-sea siliceous sponges harbor distinct and functionally diverse microbiomes.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Sponges, phylum Porifera, are long-lived and basal-branching metazoans that play important roles in ocean biogeochemistry and host diverse microbial communities. Siliceous sponges form a major clade of the Porifera; however, their microbiome is not well characterized, particularly in the deep ocean. Here, we used shotgun metagenomics to investigate the composition of the microbial communities of 13 siliceous sponges collected from four sites near Puerto Rico from depths ranging from 400 to 1,900 meters. Nine of the sponges in this study are from five sponge families that have not previously been sequenced using shotgun metagenomics. We assembled a total of 176 metagenome-assembled genomes from 20 bacterial phyla and 1 archaeal phylum. Ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) Nitrosopumilaceae dominated most siliceous sponge microbial communities and was strikingly the sole symbiont associated with one sponge (Farrea). Overall, microbiome diversity was relatively low across siliceous sponges, except for a Phloeodictyidae, which is likely a high microbial abundance (HMA) sponge. Our results suggest that host sponge phylogeny may shape microbial community structure, with limited evidence for an environmental role. The sponge-associated microbial communities contained genetic capabilities for diverse metabolic functions, particularly contributing to the carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycles. In addition to the AOA, evidence of potential for microbial autotrophy was found through the presence of genes for RuBisCO, methanotrophy, and ATP citrate lyase. These results reveal both conserved relationships and metabolic flexibility across siliceous sponge lineages, suggesting unique evolutionary dynamics and demonstrating the importance of microbial metabolism to sponge host health and nutrient cycling in the oligotrophic deep ocean.IMPORTANCEMarine sponges, emerging ~600 million years ago, have close relationships with microorganisms, but the microbiome of deep-sea siliceous sponges is not well understood. Siliceous sponges play essential roles in deep-sea ecosystems by providing habitats for other metazoans and mediating carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling; however, they remain some of the least-studied sponges. By shotgun sequencing DNA from 13 siliceous sponges collected near Puerto Rico, this study found that host sponge phylogeny is linked to microbial community composition and structure. Ammonia-oxidizing archaea dominated the microbial communities associated with marine sponges, likely playing key roles in utilizing metabolic byproducts and supporting host health. Other microbes also contributed to nutrient cycling and contained the potential to fix carbon, suggesting metabolic flexibility, which may benefit sponge hosts in low-resource environments. These findings emphasize the ecological importance of siliceous sponge-microbe symbioses and contribute to our understanding of the drivers shaping their structure and function.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Degradation of (S)-1,3-butanediol in Pseudomonas putida KT2440 reveals a CoA-activation route and enantiomeric crosstalk between (R)- and (S)-3-hydroxybutyrate catabolism.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: 1,3-Butanediol (1,3-BDO) exists as (R)- and (S)-enantiomers, yet how aerobic bacteria catabolize the (S)-form has been unknown. Here, we define (S)-1,3-BDO degradation pathway in Pseudomonas putida KT2440 and uncover an enantioselective enzyme that both controls the pathway and enables a chiral resolution. Transcriptomics, quantitative RT-PCR, and systematic gene deletions show that the ped cluster oxidizes (S)-1,3-BDO to (S)-3-hydroxybutyrate [(S)-3-HB] using the same upstream machinery as (R)-1,3-BDO and 1,4-BDO, but that the downstream route then diverges sharply. Rather than the free-acid dehydrogenase route used for (R)-3-HB, (S)-3-HB is catabolized through an acyl-CoA synthetase, Acs (PP_3458): a Δacs mutant cannot grow on (S)-3-HB, and complementation restores growth, establishing that PP_3458 activates (S)-3-HB to (S)-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA for β-oxidation. This ATP-dependent CoA-activation route is mechanistically distinct from the ATP-independent (S)-3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (3SHBDH) pathway of anaerobic Clostridia, identifying a different enzymatic solution to (S)-3-HB assimilation in aerobes. We further show that PP_3458 strongly prefers (S)- over (R)-3-HB and is inhibited by (R)-3-HB, a crosstalk that explains why a (R)-3-HB-accumulating mutant arrests on racemic 3-HB. Two applications follow directly: whole-cell kinetic resolution that converts racemic 3-HB to (S)-3-HB at high enantiomeric excess (ee > 0.99), and, in a strain unable to degrade (S)-3-HB, near-quantitative recovery-providing a chiral pharmaceutical building block; and ped-based biosensors that report 1,3-BDO across both enantiomers and function in P. putida and Escherichia coli. Some mechanistic details-the inhibition mode and the individual downstream β-oxidation steps-remain to be fully resolved.IMPORTANCE1,3-Butanediol is a commercially important C4 diol, but the microbial fate of its (S)-enantiomer in aerobic bacteria has been a gap in our understanding of diol metabolism. We show that Pseudomonas putida KT2440 degrades (S)-1,3-BDO through a route that, after a shared ped-dependent oxidation to (S)-3-hydroxybutyrate, depends on an acyl-CoA synthetase (PP_3458) to activate the (S)-acid as its CoA thioester. This ATP-dependent CoA-activation step is a distinct enzymatic strategy from the ATP-independent dehydrogenase route that anaerobic bacteria use for the same substrate, showing that aerobes and anaerobes solve (S)-3-HB assimilation differently. The work also turns this enzymology into utility: because PP_3458 is enantioselective and is inhibited by (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate, the strain can be used for whole-cell kinetic resolution that yields enantiopure (S)-3-hydroxybutyrate-a chiral pharmaceutical building block-from racemic 3-hydroxybutyrate, and the ped-based biosensors reported here detect 1,3-BDO in both P. putida and Escherichia coli, providing a portable tool for strain screening.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Enhanced production of nanofibrillated bacterial cellulose through regulation of gluconic acid metabolism.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Efficient and robust bacterial cellulose production is essential for advancing the sustainable bioeconomy. In this study, we investigated the impacts of the metabolism of organic acids, mainly gluconic acid (GA), on nanofibrillated bacterial cellulose (NFBC) production by Komagataeibacter intermedius NEDO-01 under various culture conditions in aerated stirred-tank reactors. In cultures of the wild-type strain in a standard medium, rapid GA production decreased the medium pH and depleted glucose, inhibiting cell growth and reducing the NFBC yield. However, proper pH control and continuous feeding reversed these effects, resulting in a threefold increase in NFBC yield (from 2.45 to 7.59 g/L). In cultures of a glucose dehydrogenase gene-deficient (Δgcd) strain, lack of a pH drop and glucose depletion facilitated better cell growth, yielding 1.85 times more NFBC than that in wild-type cultures under pH-uncontrolled no-feed conditions (4.53 g/L). Notably, GA supplementation accelerated cell growth but significantly inhibited NFBC synthesis, suggesting that GA uptake redirects the carbon flux toward central metabolism. In the corn steep liquor (Csl)-based medium, cell growth was significantly enhanced, and NFBC yield was equivalent to or higher than that obtained with the Hestrin-Shramm medium. GA accumulation was markedly reduced, suppressing pH fluctuation. Under these optimized conditions, three molasses types were tested with Csl, yielding relatively high NFBC. Structural analysis of NFBC produced using these alternative media revealed slight differences in the fiber width distribution, with crystallinity and fiber width remaining constant. Overall, NFBC of consistent quality can be produced in stirred-tank reactors using Komagataeibacter spp. from various agricultural by-products. [IMPORTANCE] In this study, we investigated the interplay between organic acid metabolism and nanofibrillated bacterial cellulose (NFBC) production in stirred-tank reactor cultures of Komagataeibacter intermedius NEDO-01. While it is well known that gluconic acid production competes with cellulose biosynthesis in Komagataeibacter, the quantitative relationship between these pathways under varying culture conditions has not been fully elucidated. By applying optimized feeding strategies and employing a glucose dehydrogenase knockout mutant, we demonstrated that suppressing gluconic acid accumulation significantly enhances NFBC yield. Furthermore, we explored the use of agro-industrial by-products, including molasses and corn steep liquor, as alternative, low-cost feedstocks. Structural characterization confirmed that NFBCs produced under these conditions maintained consistent quality. These findings contribute to the development of scalable, cost-effective microbial production processes for nanocellulose, which is essential for advancing the sustainable bioeconomy.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Monitoring disease trends and characterization of non-typhoidal Salmonella isolates from community wastewater in a mid-sized city in Florida, USA: a retrospective study.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) poses a serious threat for multi-drug-resistant infections in the United States. However, most infections are not detected through traditional clinical surveillance, which severely underestimates the community disease burden. Wastewater-based epidemiology can overcome barriers in clinical surveillance and fill the gap. We performed a retrospective study to monitor disease trends and characterize viable NTS isolates from a medium-sized city's wastewater treatment plants. Of 106 weekly raw influent samples from September 2020 to September 2021, 81 samples (76.42%) were NTS-positive via qPCR. NTS wastewater trends were a leading indicator of salmonellosis hospitalizations in the community by 1 week. The 27 unique NTS isolates (representing 11 different serotypes) recovered from wastewater revealed the biodiversity of community circulating infections. Wastewater samples showed a lower biodiversity of serotypes than environmental samples. The biodiversity of isolates collected from wastewater and clinical surveillance was similar but also represented serotypes not identified through traditional clinical surveillance approaches. Genotypic profiles of wastewater isolates revealed that many isolates have the potential for multi-drug-resistant infections and contain virulence genes associated with severe disease. This study shows that wastewater-based epidemiology is a valuable tool for monitoring disease trends and can provide early warning signs of salmonellosis in a community. We successfully enriched and cultured viable NTS isolates from raw wastewater samples frozen for over 1 year, further expanding the capabilities of retrospective studies allowing for future characterization of isolates. Overall, wastewater-based epidemiology is a powerful tool for retrospective analysis and for real-time community surveillance of NTS. [IMPORTANCE] Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) is an emerging tool for community-level infectious disease surveillance, yet its application to bacterial pathogens remains largely underexplored. Our study demonstrated that WBE effectively tracks non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) trends, serving as a leading indicator of hospitalizations. We successfully recovered and characterized Salmonella isolates from wastewater, highlighting its potential for genomic surveillance. We found that NTS remains viable in frozen wastewater samples for up to 1 year, the longest reported storage time to date. Characterizing bacterial isolates allows for studying pathogen evolution, AMR dynamics, and source tracking. Expanding WBE applications to bacteria could significantly enhance our understanding of disease dynamics and inform proactive public health interventions. Further research is needed to validate WBE as an early warning system for bacterial diseases and integration into a One Health framework. Our findings highlight WBE's growing role in infectious disease epidemiology, reinforcing its value as a powerful public health surveillance tool.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Integrated genomics and metabolomics survey of steroids from myxobacteria.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Steroids from myxobacteria remain largely underexplored compared to other natural product classes, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of their biosynthetic diversity, evolutionary trajectories, and pharmacological potential. To address this, we conducted a systematic genomic survey of myxobacterial genomes to delineate the distribution and phylogenetic context of sterol biosynthetic genes, which we found to be organized in a dispersed manner across the chromosome rather than clustered into canonical biosynthetic gene clusters. While the sterol biosynthetic machinery is broadly distributed across Myxococcota, its occurrence is strikingly uneven among lineages, with Nannocystaceae exhibiting the highest biosynthetic potential. Sequence similarity network mining of the oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs) essential for sterol biosynthesis revealed extensive sequence divergence and unexplored space for discovering novel catalytic functions. Motivated by these bioinformatics predictions, we further demonstrated that integrated chromatographic pre-fractionation with NMR-based metabolic profiling streamlines the targeted isolation of steroids. This approach yielded 12 (seco-)steroids from 2 in-house myxobacterial strains, including 4 previously undescribed structures featuring diverse oxidative decorations, skeletal rearrangements, and ring degradation. Bioactivity assays uncovered that a co-produced metabolite alkylglycoside synergistically potentiates the antimicrobial activity of select secosteroids. Collectively, this study establishes an integrated genomics-metabolomics pipeline that not only expands the structural repertoire of myxobacterial steroids but also provides a blueprint for future discovery of cryptic sterol metabolites and their hidden biological functions.IMPORTANCEThis study presents a systematic phylogenomic survey of sterol biosynthetic genes across the phylum Myxococcota, revealing a dispersed genomic architecture that diverges from canonical bacterial secondary metabolite gene clusters. Beyond this conceptual advance, we demonstrate, for the first time, that NMR-based metabolomics coupled with chromatographic pre-fractionation can accelerate steroid discovery from myxobacteria, leading to the discovery of previously undescribed (seco-)steroids that expand the known chemical space. This integrated pipeline not only enables efficient discovery of cryptic sterol metabolites but also establishes a foundation for understanding the ecological roles of steroids in myxobacteria.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: SzMBL1, a metallo-β-lactamase gene in Sarocladium zeae, confers tolerance to the maize phytoanticipin 2-benzoxazolinone.
