Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Maize produces pre-formed secondary metabolites with antimicrobial and invertebrate anti-herbivory properties. Fusarium verticillioides, a mycotoxigenic maize pathogen, detoxifies the maize phytoanticipin 2-benzoxazolinone (BOA) through gene action of FvMBL1, which encodes a putative metallo-β-lactamase within the FDB1 gene cluster. This cluster is also present in other maize-colonizing fungi, including the pathogen Colletotrichum graminicola and, as reported here, the protective endophyte Sarocladium zeae, which exhibits antagonistic activity against mycotoxigenic fungi. The role of the FvMBL1 ortholog in S. zeae, designated SzMBL1, was assessed by gene deletion and add-back complementation. Deletion of SzMBL1 rendered S. zeae incapable of degrading BOA and therefore unable to grow on BOA-amended medium, whereas complemented add-back strains restored BOA tolerance and, in some cases, enhanced growth at higher concentrations of BOA. Quantitative PCR analyses revealed higher copy numbers and expression levels in all add-back transformants relative to the wild type, consistent with their enhanced growth. HPLC-MS/MS analysis further showed that SzMBL1 hydrolyzes BOA, ultimately resulting in biotransformation into the non-toxic metabolite N-(2-hydroxyphenyl)malonamic acid (HPMA). Together, this study confirms the conserved function of the SzMBL1 gene involved in BOA detoxification. This study suggests that the FDB1 gene cluster, harboring SzMBL1 in S. zeae, was likely transferred through horizontal gene transfer between maize-colonizing fungi and plays a role in the degradation of host-derived secondary metabolites that function as filters limiting which fungi are most frequently associated with maize.IMPORTANCEMaize produces secondary metabolites such as 2-benzoxazolinone (BOA) to help protect against microbes and insects. The pathogenic Fusarium verticillioides carries FvMBL1, a gene within the FDB1 gene cluster that helps break down BOA. This cluster is also present in other maize-associated fungi such as Colletotrichum graminicola and, as reported here, the protective fungus Sarocladium zeae. In our experiments, when a gene similar to FvMBL1, denoted SzMBL1, is deleted in S. zeae, the fungus could no longer break down BOA or grow on BOA-amended medium. Complementation restored BOA tolerance and growth phenotypes. Notably, some S. zeae add-back strains showed increased growth at higher BOA concentrations. Our analysis showed that these hypertolerant complemented strains had multiple, transcriptionally active copies of SzMBL1. The study highlights the role of SzMBL1 in BOA detoxification, thereby aiding fungal tolerance to antimicrobial compounds, and supports the hypothesis that the FDB1 gene cluster can be horizontally transferred among maize-colonizing fungi.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Microbiomes of soils and leafy vegetables in urban agriculture systems reflect crop management and local environmental conditions.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Soil and plant microbiomes influence crop quality and preharvest food safety, yet these processes have been largely unexplored in urban agriculture environments. Here, we investigated how the microbiota of soil and leafy greens (e.g., kale, lettuce, chard, and cabbage) interact with site-specific management practices and environmental conditions across seven urban agriculture sites in the greater Washington, DC, area. Samples of leaf tissue (n = 92), rhizosphere soil (n = 92), and "native" or bulk soil (n = 39) were collected and analyzed with 16S rRNA gene and ITS2 genomic region amplicon sequencing. Microbial community composition varied significantly across sites for all sample types, as influenced by irrigation water source (i.e., municipal vs natural water), crop type, soil pH, soil moisture content, and climatic conditions (i.e., rainfall, temperature). Rhizosphere soils harbored the most bacterial taxa known to respond to organic inputs (e.g., Massilia and various members of Firmicutes and Verrucomicrobiota), whereas fungal networks dominated by saprotrophic members of Ascomycota were more stable in the bulk soils. Source-tracking analysis indicated that the phyllosphere microbiota, although variable and transient in composition, were largely derived from the rhizosphere soil. Notably, leafy greens at some sites were enriched with taxa associated with biocontrol potential (e.g., Lactobacillaceae). Moreover, machine learning models yielded strong performance in predicting specific production sites based on the bacterial communities in the rhizosphere and phyllosphere, suggesting possible microbiome-based applications for food traceability. Collectively, these findings demonstrate how local environments and crop management practices shape preharvest leafy green microbiomes in urban production.IMPORTANCEUrban farming and gardening are rapidly expanding to support local communities and enhance food security, yet these small-scale food systems are often established in uniquely developed landscapes and with resource-dependent operations. This study shows that complex site-specific factors influence the soil and leafy green microbiomes in urban agriculture systems. Our findings have important implications for future efforts in targeted farm management to enhance sustainable production and preharvest food safety.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Pseudomonas enhances soil phosphorus bioavailability and maize seedling growth and affects soil microbial community.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The low bioavailability of phosphorus in soil is a significant limiting factor for crop production, and inoculation with phosphate-solubilizing bacteria (PSB) has been recognized as an effective method. In this study, two strains with high phosphate-solubilizing ability, namely, Pseudomonas veronii 1416X3 and Pseudomonas sp. 1616X1, were obtained and used in pot experiments to investigate the effects of strains on phosphorus content in soil, maize plant growth, and soil microbial community. Results showed that after 4-day post-inoculation with PSB, the content of available phosphorus in the 1416X3 group (8.11 mg/L) and the 1616X1 group (6.77 mg/L) was significantly higher than that in the control group (4.97 mg/L), increasing by 1.63- and 1.36-fold, respectively. After inoculation with PSB, the microbial community of the soil rhizosphere was varied. In the 1416X3 group, shifts in the microbial community were characterized by increased relative abundances of Arthrobacter and Nocardioides, while in the 1616X1 group, the bacterial strain alters the microbial community through effective colonization and phosphate solubilization. To further elucidate the mechanisms underlying phosphorus solubilization of Pseudomonas, whole-genome sequencing of P. veronii 1416X3 and Pseudomonas sp. 1616X1 was investigated. The results revealed several genes associated with phosphate solubilization metabolism and phosphorus transport systems (pstSCAB-phoU), as well as organic acid production (gcd, pqqB-F, mqo, and ttuC). Therefore, this study establishes a basis for utilizing Pseudomonas strains as microbial phosphorus fertilizers, offering an effective and eco-friendly alternative in the pursuit of sustainable agriculture. [IMPORTANCE] This study identified two Pseudomonas strains capable of efficiently activating soil phosphorus and significantly promoting maize growth. It revealed their synergistic biological mechanisms involving colonization competition, organic acid secretion, and phosphorus transport systems. The research not only provides high-quality microbial resources for developing bio-phosphate fertilizers based on indigenous functional strains but also offers a theoretical foundation and technical pathway for addressing the challenge of "high total phosphorus reserve but low available phosphorus supply" in soil, reducing the dependence on chemical phosphate fertilizers, and advancing green agricultural development.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Impacts of temperature on hydrogenotrophic denitrifying aquifer microbiota.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Groundwater is a globally relevant drinking water resource, yet nitrate pollution from agriculture increasingly threatens its quality, especially in shallow, oxygen-rich aquifers where natural attenuation is limited. This study examined whether gaseous hydrogen can stimulate autochthonous chemolithoautotrophic denitrification in nitrate-polluted, gravel aquifer sediments, and whether this process remains effective across temperatures relevant for laboratory and field conditions. We hypothesized that both microbial community composition and the kinetics of nitrate reduction will change under distinct temperature regimes. Microcosm incubations of sediments from a nitrate-polluted aquifer successfully enriched native hydrogenotrophic denitrifiers. Denitrification activity was quantified at 12°C, 15°C, 20°C, and 25°C, with maximum rates ranging from ~1 to ~1.8 µmol g⁻¹ sediment day⁻¹, and average rates generally following the expected kinetic temperature responses. Higher temperatures supported greater microbial biomass and community diversity, including a broader range of denitrifiers. Nevertheless, a single population, a novel strain of Acidovorax defluvii, dominated the community across all temperatures. Unlike the heterotrophic type strain, it possessed a conserved, likely transferable gene cluster for hydrogen oxidation, hydrogen sensing, and CO₂ fixation, as revealed by metagenomics. Although complete denitrifiers with hydrogen-oxidation capacity dominated at all temperatures, nitrite accumulated transiently below 15°C. The presence of aerobic respiration genes in all enriched denitrifiers indicates their ability to switch to oxygen as an electron acceptor if available. Our study demonstrates a notable presence of an autochthonous hydrogenotrophic denitrification potential in the studied aquifer and its effective stimulation by hydrogen injection alone. Furthermore, it identifies mass transfer constraints and redox control as targets for future process optimization.IMPORTANCENitrate contamination of groundwater remains a widespread challenge in agricultural regions, and effective in situ remediation strategies are urgently needed. Hydrogen-stimulated chemolithoautotrophic denitrification represents a promising, low-carbon approach, yet its robustness under environmentally relevant temperature conditions has remained unclear. Our findings show that indigenous aquifer microorganisms can rapidly and consistently perform hydrogenotrophic denitrification across a broad temperature range (12-25°C), driven by a dominant Acidovorax species with a specialized hydrogen-oxidizing gene cluster. Identification of a conserved, potentially transferable gene cluster conferring chemolithoautotrophic lifestyle is not only biotechnologically interesting but also contributes to debate about genomic and ecological definitions of microbial species. This demonstrates that hydrogen injection can reliably activate existing microbial potential without requiring bioaugmentation and that temperature-driven shifts in community composition do not compromise nitrate removal. These insights advance the development of hydrogen-based bioremediation strategies for nitrate-impacted aquifers.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Pyridoxine can inhibit salvage of other B(6) vitamers in Salmonella enterica.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) is a nutrient required by all life. As an essential cofactor, PLP powers enzymatic reactions in primary and secondary metabolism. Microbes can obtain PLP through either de novo PLP biosynthesis or the salvage of exogenous vitamin B6. Vitamin B6 exists in multiple forms (vitamers) in the natural environment, but the effect of mixed B6 vitamer supplementation on microbial physiology has not been explored. In this study, the ability of Salmonella enterica to obtain PLP during growth in media containing various ratios of B6 vitamers is examined. The data show that the B6 vitamer, pyridoxine (PN), can inhibit the salvage of B6 vitamers, pyridoxamine and pyridoxal, by S. enterica pdxH mutants. Genetic analyses were performed to determine the mechanism by which PN disrupts pyridoxamine and pyridoxal salvage. Mutants resistant to PN inhibition during the salvage of pyridoxamine were isolated and found to encode variants of B6 kinase (PdxK) with altered activity toward the B6 vitamer substrates. Suppressor analysis suggests that PN inhibition is, at least, partially due to competitive inhibition of the pyridoxamine kinase activity of PdxK by PN. Additionally, the data indicate that pyridoxine 5'-phosphate (PNP)-mediated toxicity also contributes to growth inhibition by PN. [IMPORTANCE] Without successful acquisition and utilization of vitamin B6, microbes cannot survive or perform their essential roles in human health and the natural environment. Vitamin B6 exists in multiple forms (vitamers) in the natural world, but the effect of B6 vitamer mixtures on microbial growth has not been analyzed. This work shows that the B6 vitamers are not necessarily interchangeable sources of PLP, and they may have distinct effects on microbial physiology.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Autoinducer-2 functions as both a quorum-sensing and metabolic signal in Escherichia coli.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Bacteria integrate diverse environmental signals to coordinate behavior, yet the relationship between nutrient sensing and quorum sensing (QS) remains incompletely understood. Autoinducer-2 (AI-2) is unique among QS signals in that its production is tightly linked to central metabolism, raising fundamental questions about the boundary between metabolic and signaling functions. In Escherichia coli, AI-2 coordinates collective behaviors through the lsr operon, whose expression is controlled not only by the AI-2-responsive repressor LsrR but also by the cAMP receptor protein (CRP), placing it at the intersection of carbon sensing and population-level signaling. While inhibition of lsr expression by PTS sugars was previously established, we show that non-PTS sugars similarly suppress lsr expression through CRP, further decoupling QS activation from cell density and coupling it to carbon source availability. Genomic analysis across Enterobacteriaceae reveals that CRP binding sites in the lsr promoter are broadly conserved, indicating that metabolic modulation of AI-2 signaling is an ancestral regulatory feature. Using a FRET-based biosensor, we further show that AI-2 uptake modulates intracellular cAMP levels similarly to non-PTS carbon transport, suggesting AI-2 may have originally functioned as a nutrient substrate. Additionally, we isolated soil- and phyllosphere-associated bacteria capable of utilizing AI-2 as a sole carbon source. Interestingly, this capacity seems to have evolved independently from the ability to produce and metabolize AI-2 through the LuxS/Lsr pathway. Overall, our findings reveal an underappreciated metabolic basis of AI-2 QS and suggest that, in some species, nutrient utilization and intercellular signaling may have diverged from a common ancestral pathway.IMPORTANCEQuorum sensing allows bacteria to coordinate collective behaviors by detecting secreted signaling molecules, yet the evolutionary origins of these systems remain poorly understood. AI-2, one of the most broadly conserved bacterial signals, is derived from central metabolism and processed by machinery in Escherichia coli that strikingly resembles a sugar utilization system. Here, we show that nutrient availability overrides cell density as the primary determinant of AI-2 responsiveness, that this regulatory logic is conserved among Enterobacteriaceae genomes, and that environmental bacteria can grow on AI-2 as a sole carbon source. These findings reframe AI-2 as a signal embedded within, and potentially evolved from, nutrient-sensing pathways, with direct implications for understanding how byproducts of cellular metabolism can acquire signaling functions.

PLOS Biology.title: An indirect wing steering muscle stabilizes flight by regulating wing pitch angle in Drosophila
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Han Kheng Teoh, Debojyoti Biswas, Haoru Li, Abby Leung, B. Kemper Ludlow, Samuel C. Whitehead, Erica Ehrhardt, Michael Dickinson, Tsevi Beatus, Noah J. Cowan, Itai Cohen Flapping flight is inherently unstable, requiring Drosophila to fine-tune their wing motions on a milliseconds timescale. Pioneering studies have shown that the direct steering muscles, which attach to the wing hinge, are important for generating these rapid flight reflexes. Recent connectome data, however, reveal that indirect steering muscles or tension muscles, which alter the mechanics of the thorax, receive some of the same synaptic inputs from the sensory apparatus as the direct steering muscles. This discovery suggests that the indirect steering muscles may also be important for flight control. Here, we show that the indirect tergopleural muscles indeed contribute substantially to stabilization, particularly for large pitch perturbations. We find that for small perturbations (less than 1,000 °/s), flies modulate their wing stroke amplitude to generate lift-based corrective torques, a strategy that has been previously documented. For larger perturbations, however, we observe that Drosophila engage an additional wing degree of freedom—the wing pitch angle—to leverage additional lift and drag forces during the corrective maneuver. Quasi-steady aerodynamic simulations reveal that this strategy minimizes power consumption, anaolgous to how some mammals (including humans) adjust their steady-state gaits in a near energy-optimal manner. Using optogenetics and a control theory framework, we demonstrate that the tergopleural muscle is activated by a proportional gain component of a nonlinear proportional-integral controller responsible for determining the wing pitch angle during large perturbations. A simplified torsional spring model for the wing hinge captures the changes in the wing pitch dynamics observed during correction maneuvers by using the tergopleural muscle to adjust the rest angle of the wing. These findings provide a striking example of reflex strategy selection in time-critical behaviors and underscore the vital role of indirect steering muscles in flight stabilization.

mBio.title: Electron cryo-tomography reveals the Caulobacter vibrioides tight-adherence pilus machine architecture.
mBio.abstract: The type IV filament superfamily is a widespread group of molecular machines involved in natural transformation, motility, adhesion, nutrient uptake, and secretion of a wide spectrum of protein substrates. The gram-negative bacterium Caulobacter vibrioides expresses the tight-adherence (Tad) pilus, a type IV machine involved in surface colonization. Here, we investigated the proteins involved in Tad pilus production by ΦCbK resistance screening and the order of machine assembly and its polar remnant by fluorescence tagging. Using electron cryo electron tomography and subtomogram averaging of wild-type and mutant strains, we resolved the Tad pilus machine architecture and built an integrative model of its structure. The resulting model suggests the individual roles of multiple Tad proteins. Together, the data also reveal the Tad pilus machine's assembly order.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria rely on microscopic, hair-like appendages, called pili, for survival and infection of host cells. Pili are separated into several structural families, the type IV tight-adherence (Tad) pilus, which help bacteria like Caulobacter vibrioides attach to surfaces of host tissues and prey cells. Despite its critical role in bacterial infection, the exact structure of the Tad pilus and the machine that assembles it is not fully understood. Understanding the structure and function of the Tad pilus and its machine is a developing conversation between genetics, bioinformatics, biochemistry, microscopy, and structure-predicting artificial intelligence (AI) programs. In this study, we combined all this information with our own advanced cell-imaging technology (cryo-ET) to add another layer of understanding to how the Tad pilus machine is organized. This model suggests dozens of hypotheses to be tested in the future and represents the next step forward in understanding the structure and function of Tad pili.

mSphere.title: High-depth whole-genome sequencing of blood culture plates reveals evolutionary dynamics in cases of persistent bacteremia due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
mSphere.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) can be applied to clinical cultures to detect polyclonal variation within a single bacterial strain, enabling the tracking of within-host evolution and transmission. Culture isolates from infected patients are often sequenced as individual colonies (c-seq). To increase the sensitivity of variant detection, cultures can also be sequenced as a pool (p-seq), but the utility of this approach is not clear for most clinical specimens. To understand how these methods perform in bacteremia, we applied p-seq to blood culture plates for 10 patients with persistent bacteremia due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. For comparison, we also applied c-seq to five colonies (c5-seq) from the same plates for six patients. p-seq was more sensitive than c5-seq for detecting low-frequency variant alleles; however, the most important factor for new variant detection was the number of culture plates analyzed, rather than the sequencing method used. We also used these data to construct Muller plots for three patients with especially diverse infecting populations, enabling the visualization of rapid evolutionary dynamics in response to antibiotic exposures. We identified 204 unique variant alleles, and our analysis provides additional evidence for parallel evolution of several different genes during S. aureus bacteremia, including genes linked to antibiotic evasion (rpoB and vraS), metabolism (pdxK), energy production (qoxA), and virulence (saeS). Overall, these data provide a detailed view of evolutionary dynamics during clinical cases of MRSA bacteremia and describe the merits and limitations of c-seq vs p-seq strategies for analyzing blood culture plates using WGS.IMPORTANCEAs bacterial whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is increasingly used as a research tool for clinical samples, it is important to understand the pros and cons of different culture sampling methodologies. Here, we analyzed cases of persistent bacteremia due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) by applying WGS of either five individual colonies isolated on blood culture plates (c5-seq) or the pooled bacterial population on each plate (p-seq). We found that p-seq was more sensitive for allele detection, but that c5-seq was better suited to understand evolutionary dynamics. Our analysis also provided evidence for the evolution of specific genetic loci of MRSA that are involved in antibiotic evasion, metabolism, energy production, and virulence. Finally, examination of patient-level factors suggests prosthetic valve endocarditis and severe immunosuppression may be risk factors for polyclonal bacteremia.

Microbiological Research.title: Learning from nature: What non-native halophilic and halotolerant bacteria reveal about root immunity under salt stress.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Soil salinity is increasingly recognised as one of the main limits to crop production worldwide, yet attempts to use halophilic and halotolerant plant growth-promoting bacteria in saline agriculture have produced mixed and often disappointing results, particularly when strains are moved onto non-native host plants. In this review, the literature is brought together to examine how such non-native halophilic and halotolerant bacteria behave at the root-soil interface under salt stress, and which molecular, physiological, and ecological factors determine whether they are rejected by, or can pass through, plant defence barriers. The article first summarises how salinity reshapes root immune organisation, from root system architecture and cell-wall properties to redox homeostasis and ABA-SA-JA signalling, and how these changes open and close specific spatial and temporal windows for microbial entry, recognition and persistence. Plant immune responses to native and non‑native halophilic bacteria are compared, revealing that differences in MAMP perception, PTI dynamics, and host-microbe feedback determine host preference and colonisation in saline rhizospheres. These findings are summarised in a mechanistic model describing six main bacterial tactics that modulate recognition, signalling, oxidative stress, hormonal balance, and cell‑wall-apoplast properties to evade or adjust host immunity. Looking across different plant-bacteria pairs and experimental setups, the review discusses why promising halophilic inoculants so often fail when transferred to new hosts, which trait combinations are repeatedly associated with successful non-native colonisation, and where the major gaps remain in in planta and systems-level evidence. Together, these points are used to argue that future microbiome-based strategies for salt-affected soils need to be designed around plant immune architecture, salinity-induced physiological states and ecological fit, rather than relying only on generic stress-alleviating traits.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: A statistical framework to identify gene-gene interactions underlying multiple dichotomous phenotypes from genotype data
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Siru Wang, Xuhui Zhu, Yu Li, Gengjie Jia Identifying gene-gene (G × G) interactions across multiple dichotomous phenotypes is challenging due to the extreme sparsity of SNP-derived interaction matrices and the reduced statistical power associated with binary outcomes. Existing G × G association methods are restricted to either single or multiple continuous phenotypes. Here we introduce GiMat (Gene Interaction and Multiple-phenotype Association Test), a statistical framework that extends multivariate kernel regression to model G × G interactions jointly across dichotomous phenotypes, while explicitly capturing homogeneous and heterogeneous interaction effects. Extensive simulations demonstrate that GiMat controls type I error conservatively and adapts power flexibly to different types of relationships between interaction effects and phenotypes. Applied to type 2 diabetes and hypertension comorbidity in the UK Biobank, GiMat identified four previously unreported G × G interaction pairs associated with both phenotypes. This scalable framework enables robust discovery of complex genetic interactions underlying multiple correlated phenotypes.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Aging out of the blue: Region-specific epigenetic clock calibration for a blue zone with the DNAm SuperLearner
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Nolan Gunter, Andres Cardenas, Michael Kobor, Nicole Gladish, Julie MacIsaac, Kristy Dever, David Rehkopf, William Dow, Luis Rosero-Bixby, Alan Hubbard Epigenetic clocks estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns at CpG sites, providing robust predictions of mortality and morbidity risk. “Blue zones,” regions of exceptional longevity, offer a unique opportunity to investigate how biological aging diverges from chronological age. However, standard clocks are typically trained on large, heterogeneous datasets, reflecting average population trends rather than region-specific dynamics. Using data from the Costa Rican Longevity and Healthy Aging Study (CRELES), we profiled DNA methylation from residents of the Nicoya blue zone (n = 206) and a reference population in other parts of Costa Rica (n = 875). We propose training a SuperLearner, an ensemble machine learning approach, on the non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans to optimize predictive performance across existing clocks and flexible machine learners. By its Oracle property, the SuperLearner’s weighted combination of algorithms performs asymptotically as well as the best possible combination of the candidate predictors. We then used this trained model to construct a calibrated hypothesis test comparing Epigenetic Age Acceleration (EAA) distributions between the blue zone region and the reference population. Before calibration or covariate adjustment, estimates for Nicoyans depended heavily on the chosen clock. The SuperLearner placed them about three years younger on average (R¯1=−3.05,95% CI [−3.64,−2.46]), whereas DNAmFitAge placed them almost four years older (R¯1=3.59,95% CI [3.02,4.17]). Mean calibration to non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans made estimates consistent across clocks, with an estimated EAA advantage to approximately two years (Δ^=−1.96,95% CI [−2.56,−1.37]). After age-stratified calibration within 10-year age groups, only a small EAA advantage (Δ^=−0.35,95% CI [−0.64,−0.05]) remained, concentrated among the oldest participants. This approach provides a robust and reproducible framework for estimating longevity in distinct regions when a relevant reference population is available.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Storing long-lived memories via molecular error correction: A minimal mathematical model of Crick’s memory switch
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by John J. Vastola, Tejas Ramdas, Samuel J. Gershman Cells store information in part by attaching molecular marks to proteins and DNA. But because marks can be randomly removed (e.g., due to ambient phosphatase activity) and added (e.g., due to ambient kinase activity), information encoding may be poor, and in the worst case marks may only store information on the time scale of molecular turnover. We identify a high-level strategy cells use to maintain encoding fidelity beyond the time scale of turnover—which we call molecular error correction—and find that it closely resembles an underexplored theoretical proposal by Francis Crick. To assess the effectiveness of molecular error correction, we construct and analyze several minimal mathematical models of molecular memory switches. We find that Crick-like error correction provides an efficient way to improve the lifetime of stored memories, especially compared to redundantly encoding information using a large number of molecules, but that it can yield false positives (and hence low information fidelity) when there is ambient marking activity; given these two competing concerns, the optimal level of error correction is moderate rather than arbitrarily high. We also find that combining error correction with redundant encoding can efficiently and robustly produce memories that last between ten and one hundred times longer than the turnover time scale. Our work provides insight regarding how to model and interrogate noisy molecular memory systems, suggests that error correction is a design principle of molecular memory, and quantitatively connects error correction to observable memory time scales.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Radiopharmaceutical therapy for metastatic prostate cancer: Insights from mechanistic modeling and in silico trials
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Matteo Italia, Silvia Bordel-Vozmediano, José García Otero, Gabriel F. Calvo, Víctor M. Pérez-García Radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has rapidly evolved into a key precision-oncology modality, with radioligands now approved or in late-stage development for multiple solid tumors, including neuroendocrine and prostate cancers. RPT with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA (Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen) has recently been approved as a life-prolonging treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but its clinical use still relies on nonpersonalized, empirically chosen fixed schedules. Here, we develop a mechanistic, patient-personalizable mathematical model simulating mCRPC response and organ-at-risk toxicity during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT. The model integrates tumor growth dynamics, radiobiological response, and organ-resolved pharmacokinetics inferred from mass data and standardized uptake values obtained from positron emission tomography studies. Parameters were derived from the literature, although the framework allows personalization by fitting to patient-specific data, such as imaging and prostate-specific antigen levels. Analytical threshold analysis identified a critical activity scale governing net tumor control, while simulations of a representative virtual patient (VP) illustrated the model’s coupled tumor and activity dynamics. Global sensitivity analysis identified tumor growth, uptake, and radiosensitivity parameters as key drivers of interpatient variability. Using VP cohorts generated via stochastic parameter sampling, we conducted in silico trials and benchmarked the model against published dosimetry and survival data for [177Lu]Lu-PSMA trials. Convergence testing supported the use of cohorts of 500 VPs for stable population-level estimates. We then explored dosing and scheduling strategies to quantify efficacy–toxicity trade-offs. Consolidated regimens with fewer, higher-activity injections improved overall survival (OS) in silico but increased toxicity, especially in kidneys. Cycle length had a weaker influence on OS within a 2–9 week window, while it clearly affected toxicity, whereas excessive delays (> 12 weeks) markedly reduced efficacy. These methodological findings illustrate how mechanistic modeling and in silico trials can inform the design and personalization of RPT regimens.

Environmental Science & Technology.title: Environmentally Relevant F-53B Exposure Triggers Ovarian Cancer Progression via C5aR1-Mediated Noncanonical Signaling: An Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) Underlying Hybrid EMT and Stemness.
Environmental Science & Technology.abstract: Significant gaps remain in the health risk assessment methodologies for the PFOS (perfluorooctanesulfonic acid) alternative 6:2 Cl-PFESA (6:2 chlorinated polyfluoroalkyl ether sulfonate, F-53B), which has been widely recognized as the alternative to PFOS in China. To address this research gap, our study integrated multidimensional techniques to mechanistically construct an Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) for F-53B-induced ovarian cancer progression. Our findings demonstrated that exposure to environmentally relevant concentrations of F-53B significantly enhanced the migratory and invasive capabilities of ovarian cancer cells. Within the AOP framework of F-53B-induced hybrid epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and enhanced tumor stemness, the upregulation of C5aR1─triggered by ERα acting as a noncanonical receptor of F-53B─constitutes the molecular initiating event (MIE). Following this MIE, the recruitment of β-arrestin1 and Src was induced, leading to the assembly of a C5aR1/β-arrestin1/Src signaling complex. This complex facilitated the binding of β-arrestin1 to β-catenin and drove the nuclear translocation of β-catenin, ultimately activating hybrid EMT and stemness of tumor cells. Administration of the C5aR1 inhibitor PMX205 effectively abrogated subsequent key events (KEs) caused by F-53B exposure. Through in vitro and in vivo validation, our study established an AOP framework that provides a novel perspective for evaluating the potential risk of PFAS substitutes in promoting cancer progression.

Journal of Virology.title: Structural basis of avian-to-human receptor-binding adaptation in H9Ny influenza A virus hemagglutinin.
Journal of Virology.abstract: The receptor-binding specificity of influenza A virus (IAV) hemagglutinin (HA) is a major determinant for viral host tropism, enabling interspecies transmission. The molecular determinants for receptor-binding properties of HAs vary among different IAV subtypes. In this study, we performed a comprehensive analysis on the receptor-binding determinants of IAV subtype H9 HA and found that the receptor-binding characteristics of H9 subtype influenza viruses have exhibited temporal variations over decades. Q226L (hydrophobicity switch) substitution in the 220-loop is the key determinant for H9 subtype HA to acquire human receptor-binding preference. The amino acid residues of the 130-loop greatly affect the binding of HA protein to canonical receptors. Organoid infection models demonstrate that all three representative viral strains could infect human bronchial epithelial organoids. These findings increase our understanding of the molecular determinants of receptor-binding properties of different HA subtypes and call for the surveillance and response to potential influenza outbreaks, or even epidemics/pandemics.IMPORTANCEInfluenza A virus (IAV) subtype H9 poses persistent zoonotic spillover risks due to its adaptive receptor-binding capacity, yet the molecular determinants remain incompletely defined. This study systematically characterizes the receptor-binding determinants of H9 hemagglutinin over decades of viral evolution and identifies two critical functional domains: the 220-loop residue Q226L substitution, which serves as the key mutation conferring human receptor-binding preference, and the 130-loop residues that predominantly modulate canonical receptor-binding affinity. Functional assays using human bronchial epithelial organoids further confirm the robust human infection ability of prevalent H9 viral strains. These findings clarify the molecular mechanisms underlying H9 IAV host tropism and adaptive evolution, provide critical theoretical evidence for targeted influenza surveillance and pandemic preparedness against emerging H9 influenza outbreaks.

Journal of Virology.title: Hepatitis C virus remodels lipid droplets to promote mitochondrial fatty acid accumulation and metabolic activation.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) depends on host lipid metabolism and lipid droplets (LDs) for genome replication, assembly, and particle production, yet how LD structure and lipid utilization change over the course of infection remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the temporal remodeling of LD-associated metabolic pathways during HCV JFH-1 infection of human hepatoma Huh7 cells. HCV infection transiently increased LD fluorescence intensity at 24 h post-infection (hpi), followed by normalization or relative loss of LD signal at later time points. Concomitantly, LDs became progressively clustered and enlarged during late infection, despite reduced protein levels of the canonical LD fusion proteins CIDEA, CIDEB, and CIDEC, suggesting that HCV-induced LD enlargement is not associated with increased expression of CIDE proteins. Transcriptomic, RT-qPCR, and immunoblot analyses revealed time-dependent regulation of genes and proteins involved in LD structure, triglyceride synthesis, lipolysis, lipid uptake, and mitochondrial fatty acid utilization. Subcellular fractionation demonstrated preferential accumulation of fatty acids in mitochondrial fractions at 24-72 hpi. This redistribution was accompanied by increased oxygen consumption rate, elevated extracellular acidification, and progressive reactive oxygen species accumulation, indicating infection-associated metabolic activation and oxidative stress. Pharmacological inhibition of DGAT1-dependent LD biogenesis, LIPA-dependent lysosomal lipid hydrolysis, LIPE/HSL-dependent lipolysis, or CPT1-dependent mitochondrial fatty acid transport markedly reduced mitochondrial fatty acid accumulation and suppressed HCV-induced respiratory activity. Inhibition of LIPA or LIPE/HSL reduced both HCV RNA and core protein levels, whereas inhibition of CPT1 or DGAT1 had more pronounced effects on core protein than on viral RNA. Together, these findings support a model in which HCV dynamically remodels LDs, mobilizes LD-associated fatty acids, and redirects them toward mitochondria to support infection-associated metabolism and downstream stages of the viral life cycle. Lipid hydrolysis and mitochondrial fatty acid trafficking therefore represent potential host-directed targets for limiting HCV infection.IMPORTANCEHepatitis C virus depends on host lipid metabolism for replication, assembly, and production of infectious particles, but how it uses lipid droplets over time remains incompletely understood. This study shows that hepatitis C virus dynamically remodels lipid droplets, causing an early increase in lipid storage followed by droplet enlargement and mobilization of fatty acids during later infection. The released fatty acids preferentially accumulate in mitochondria, where they are associated with increased cellular respiration and oxidative stress. Blocking lipid droplet formation, lipid breakdown, or fatty acid transport to mitochondria reduced this metabolic response and decreased viral RNA or core protein accumulation. Inhibition of lysosomal acid lipase and hormone-sensitive lipase suppressed both viral RNA and protein levels. These findings identify lipid droplet breakdown and mitochondrial fatty acid trafficking as important host processes used by hepatitis C virus and as potential targets for host-directed antiviral intervention.

Journal of Virology.title: Changes in the chromatin accessibility landscape during human adenovirus infection.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Viral infections rewire the cellular environment, and this is often achieved through chromatin remodeling. Human adenovirus (HAdV) can directly modify specific cellular chromatin features; however, we still lack a global view of the changes in the cellular chromatin landscape induced during infection. To address how host chromatin accessibility changes during HAdV-C5 infection, we performed assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) in growth-arrested diploid human lung fibroblast (IMR-90) cells at 48 and 72 h post-infection. We detected widespread changes in chromatin accessibility, with 7,055 and 10,736 differentially accessible regions (DARs) on host chromatin at 48 and 72 h post-infection, respectively. At both time points, these changes mostly occurred in enhancer/intergenic regions and intronic regions. Furthermore, the pattern of changes in accessibility differed between protein-coding and non-coding genes. Integration of the ATAC-seq data with RNA-seq data demonstrated that significant changes in chromatin accessibility coincided with significant changes in gene expression during infection. Additionally, we found that increased DARs were enriched for forkhead and TEA domain transcription factor family motifs, while decreased DARs were enriched for motifs from zinc finger and basic leucine zipper domain families. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that Wnt signaling pathway genes displayed increased chromatin accessibility during infection. Inhibition of the Wnt signaling pathway reduced viral gene expression and infectious viral progeny production, suggesting that this pathway is important for productive infection. Together, these data demonstrate that cellular chromatin is extensively remodeled during HAdV infection and expand our understanding of host-cell transcriptional regulation by human adenovirus. [IMPORTANCE] Human adenovirus-C5 (HAdV-C5) infection extensively modifies the cellular transcriptome and proteome. However, other important aspects of the cellular environment, such as global changes in chromatin accessibility, have yet to be fully characterized during infection. Here, we performed assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) in infected growth-arrested diploid human lung fibroblast (IMR-90) cells at 48 and 72 h post-infection. We observed genome-wide changes in cellular chromatin accessibility and identified specific transcription factor motifs located in differentially accessible regions during infection. This work contributes another key piece to our understanding of how human adenovirus infection reprograms the host-cell environment and will inform future work directed toward specific chromatin modifications manipulated by HAdV that impact host-cell chromatin accessibility.

Journal of Virology.title: Viral reprogramming of cGAS functional states: from DNA-sensing failure to multilayered immune-evasion networks.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) detects viral and mislocalized host DNA to initiate antiviral immunity. Productive cGAS activation requires coordinated DNA accessibility and engagement, catalytic activation, higher-order assembly, and appropriate subcellular context. Viruses counteract this pathway by shielding DNA, disrupting cGAS-DNA interactions, modifying or depleting cGAS, remodeling cGAS assemblies and condensates, and exploiting nuclear regulatory mechanisms. Similar phenotypes, such as reduced production of 2'3'-cyclic GMP-AMP (2'3'-cGAMP), or loss of cGAS puncta, can arise from distinct molecular lesions, complicating mechanistic interpretation. Here, we organize viral cGAS antagonism around discrete but interconnected functional states, and emphasize the experimental evidence needed to distinguish direct inhibition from secondary effects. This framework integrates viral genome biology, host factors, cellular compartments, and infection stage to clarify conserved and context-dependent strategies of immune evasion.

Journal of Virology.title: Establishment and characterization of a recombinant VSV-based pseudotyping platform for studying RSV F-mediated entry and antibody-mediated neutralization.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a leading cause of severe lower respiratory tract disease, underscoring the need for safe, scalable platforms to evaluate neutralizing antibodies, and entry-targeting antivirals. Here, we established and characterized a vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV)-based pseudovirus neutralization assay for RSV that uses fusion (F) proteins from RSV A and RSV B strains as functional entry glycoproteins. Key assay parameters were systematically evaluated, including target cell type, F-expression plasmid input, packaging multiplicity of infection, pseudovirus inoculum, detection time point, and cell seeding density. Western blotting confirmed F expression and incorporation into pseudovirus particles, and a GFP reporter-based syncytium assay verified fusion activity. Under the selected assay conditions, the assay showed strong signal linearity, low background, and reproducible reporter readouts in HEK293T cells at 24 h post-infection. Neutralization by monoclonal antibodies targeting six major antigenic sites on RSV F (sites Ø and I-V) supported the functional preservation and accessibility of multiple neutralization-relevant epitopes on the pseudovirus surface. RSV-specific fusion inhibitors selectively blocked both pseudovirus entry and F-mediated cell-cell fusion in a dose-dependent manner, whereas SARS-CoV-2 entry inhibitors had no effect, consistent with the expected virus-specific inhibition profiles. Importantly, pseudovirus neutralization titers showed positive correlations with live-virus neutralization results in both human and mouse sera. Together, these findings establish the VSV-RSV pseudovirus neutralization assay as a robust and scalable platform for measuring F-directed neutralizing activity and for supporting vaccine evaluation, serological surveillance, monoclonal antibody characterization, and antiviral discovery.IMPORTANCERespiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial disease in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals, underscoring the need for robust assays to evaluate vaccines, antibodies, and antivirals. Authentic-virus assays remain essential because they measure neutralization in the context of intact RSV, but the involvement of multiple viral components can complicate attribution of neutralization differences specifically to F. The vesicular stomatitis virus-based pseudovirus system developed here uses F as the sole RSV envelope glycoprotein and restricts infection to a single reporter-expressing round, enabling controlled comparisons of F variants, F-directed antibodies, and entry inhibitors. Its positive correlation with authentic-virus neutralization further supports its utility as a complementary platform for mechanistic and comparative studies of RSV F-directed entry and neutralization.

Journal of Virology.title: Investigation of anti-SARS-CoV-2 multimeric bicyclic peptide inhibitors in a range of preclinical therapeutic settings.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The spread of respiratory viruses, such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2, has presented significant challenges over the last 30 years, with few effective therapeutic options available to this day. Bicyclic peptides represent a unique, modular modality in the antiviral armamentarium against future pandemics. This study utilizes tool molecules to provide a deeper evaluation of multivalent bicyclic (Bicycle) molecule efficacy in several preclinical SARS-CoV-2 challenge settings. We explore both pre-exposure prophylaxis and post-exposure therapeutic settings via subcutaneous and intranasal routes of administration. We contextualize this further in bespoke scenarios where the immune system is compromised, as well as viral transmission. Promisingly, in all studies, we observe efficacy, significantly reducing infectious viral burden at each study endpoint. These data further support the candidacy of Bicycle molecules as a differentiated antiviral therapeutic class in the context of pandemic preparedness. [IMPORTANCE] The COVID-19 pandemic triggered a rapid wave of innovation, accelerating the delivery of new vaccine technology and antiviral treatments. In our first paper, we described the discovery and molecular optimization of Bicycle molecules as a novel drug class for the potential treatment of SARS-CoV-2. Here, we have performed deeper characterization of these tool molecules in established animal models to evaluate scenarios for deployment, simulating SARS-CoV-2 transmission, testing more convenient delivery routes, such as intranasal, as well as looking at immunocompromised animals. The Bicycle molecules demonstrated positive outcomes in each of these studies and suggest that Bicycle molecules, as convenient and effective antiviral treatments, could be an important addition to help future preparedness against new viral pandemics.

Journal of Virology.title: HIV-1 and SIV virions are cleared from the blood of SIV-infected macaques with similar triphasic kinetics.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Defining the clearance kinetics of lentiviral particles is essential for understanding infection dynamics in vivo, but previous studies have yielded a >10-fold difference in the estimated clearance rate for HIV-1 in humans compared to SIV in macaques. These prior analyses often employed insensitive assays, short observation periods, disparate methodologies, and the assumption of monophasic clearance kinetics, complicating interpretation of discordant findings. Here, we investigated virion clearance by intravenously infusing non-infectious SIV, HIV-1 wild-type (WT), and envelope-negative HIV-1 (Env-) into SIV-infected macaques exhibiting a range of baseline plasma viral loads. Using highly sensitive virologic assays, we monitored infused virion clearance over eight hours across ~6 logs of dynamic range. We show that virion clearance is universally multiphasic, with triphasic models providing the best fit. SIV and HIV-1 WT were cleared with indistinguishable kinetics, including a rapid first phase (mean half-life: ~2.5 min) during which >99% of infused virus was cleared. We also identified previously undetected second and third clearance phases with progressively slower kinetics, with mean half-lives of ~17 and ~126 min (when estimable), respectively, for both SIV and HIV-1 WT. HIV-1 Env- virions showed modestly but significantly slower first-phase clearance rates, suggesting a potential role for Env in early virion clearance. Baseline viral burden did not correlate with clearance kinetics, providing no evidence for a saturable clearance capacity. Our results indicate that clearance kinetics are largely independent of viral load and virus type, suggesting that prior discrepancies stem from methodological limitations, modeling assumptions, or species-specific differences between macaques and humans. [IMPORTANCE] Accurate characterization of HIV-1 clearance from the blood is fundamental for understanding viral pathogenesis, infected-cell lifespans, and the dynamics of antiretroviral therapy-mediated suppression. Historically, distinct experimental systems suggested that HIV-1 clearance in humans is significantly slower than SIV clearance in macaques. This study resolves proposed explanations for this longstanding discrepancy by directly comparing the clearance of non-infectious SIV and HIV-1 particles from macaque blood using highly sensitive virologic assays. We demonstrate that both viruses are cleared at nearly identical rates, regardless of the total amount of virus circulating in each animal, and reveal for the first time that virion clearance is not a simple monophasic decay process but represents a complex, multiphasic process that alters how we understand viral biology. Our findings indicate that previous disparities were likely driven by technological limitations, monophasic modeling assumptions, and/or species-specific differences rather than virus-specific differences or a saturable virion clearance mechanism.

Journal of Virology.title: Primer: Virus entry and uncoating.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Viruses deliver their genetic material to a replication site in the host cell to initiate infection. To accomplish this task, viruses must co-opt cellular factors to promote the steps of virus entry and uncoating. This Primer highlights how select DNA and RNA viruses accomplish these steps. Consistent themes, unresolved questions, and potential therapeutic implications are discussed.

authors: Daniel P. Leman, Brian A. Cary, Wei Wen, Brian J. Lane, Diane Bissen, Nicole F. Wong, M. Regis Shanley, Krish B. Bhut, Gina G. Turrigiano
Current Biology.abstract: Leman et al. find that rapid, vision-dependent learning triggers a slow resetting of firing rate set points in visual cortex. Thus, learning can co-opt homeostatic plasticity to reset firing rate setpoints and enhance consolidation.

Assessment of Ebola virus persistence in vitreous fluid of Ebola virus disease survivors with vitreoretinal disease in Sierra Leone: a cross-sectional study.
Lancet Microbe.abstract: [BACKGROUND] Uveitis is a known ocular manifestation in individuals who have survived Ebola virus disease (EVD). However, whether Ebola virus (EBOV; Orthoebolavirus zairense) persistence in vitreous fluid contributes to long-term sequelae of uveitis in EVD survivors remains unclear. We aimed to characterise the clinical findings and molecular and immunological findings in vitreous fluid from EVD survivors undergoing vitreoretinal surgery. [METHODS] This cross-sectional study recruited EVD survivors (cohort 1), household close contacts of EVD survivors (cohort 2), and non-EVD patients with uveitis (cohort 3) from the Sierra Leone Ministry of Health's Department of Ophthalmology or from the ongoing Sierra Leone Ministry of Health and the Lowell and Ruth Gess Eye Hospital Ebola Survivor Study (SMILE Study). EVD survivor status was based on an Ebola treatment unit certificate and confirmation in the Sierra Leone Association of Ebola Survivors registry, as well as an anti-EBOV assay. Close contacts of EVD survivors were individuals who lived in the same household as patients with EVD during the acute stage of the disease. Non-EVD patients with uveitis were individuals with vitreoretinal disease indications who were anticipated to benefit from surgical intervention. All patients had a comprehensive ophthalmic examination and pars plana vitrectomy with collection of vitreous fluid. These samples were investigated for molecular detection of EBOV RNA via quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) and evaluation of Goldmann-Witmer coefficients (GWCs) to identify intraocular production of EBOV-binding antibodies. Statistical analyses were performed to compare basic ophthalmic variables, demographic data, and GWC between the three groups. [FINDINGS] From Jan 1, 2023, to Jan 1, 2024, a total of 25 patients (cohort 1 n=10, cohort 2 n=5, cohort 3 n=10) were enrolled. 13 (52%) patients were female, and median age was 39 years (IQR 34·0-53·5). The median time from EVD symptom onset to surgery was 108·5 months (IQR 103·8-110·8) in cohort 1, and the median time from close contact with a patient with EVD to surgery was 106·0 months (IQR 103·0-106·0) in cohort 2. EBOV RNA was detected by qRT-PCR in the vitreous fluid of two (20%) of ten EVD survivors. GWCs for EBOV glycoprotein IgG were significantly elevated (median 3·59, IQR 0·93-12·53, p<0·005 for between-group comparisons) in EVD survivors compared with those in close contacts (median 0, IQR 0-2·2) and patients with uveitis (median 0, IQR 0-0·62). [INTERPRETATION] The detection of virus-specific immune responses and viral RNA at a median of 9 years after EVD diagnosis suggests long-term EBOV RNA persistence in the vitreous fluid of EVD survivors with vitreoretinal disease. Microbiology Spectrum.title: Phage display identification of MCR-1-targeting nanobodies to restore colistin susceptibility.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: The spread of antimicrobial resistance among gram-negative bacilli, particularly within Enterobacteriaceae and non-fermentative gram-negative bacilli, poses a serious and escalating threat to global public health. Colistin, a cationic antimicrobial peptide, remains a last-line treatment for infections caused by multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria. However, the global dissemination of the plasmid-encoded colistin resistance gene mobilized colistin resistance-1 (mcr-1) has contributed to increasing cases of colistin resistance and threatens global health. Nanobodies offer advantages, including high affinity, stability, and small size. Here, we isolated anti-MCR-1.1 nanobodies from a phage-display library and evaluated their potential to restore colistin efficacy. The periplasmic catalytic domain of MCR-1.1 was purified by affinity chromatography and used to immunize alpacas, resulting in the construction of a phage-displayed nanobody library against MCR-1.1 with a size of 5.8 × 10⁸ CFU. After biopanning, several anti-MCR-1.1 nanobodies specific for the periplasmic catalytic domain of MCR-1.1 were successfully isolated. Among them, high-affinity nanobodies Nb7, Nb12, Nb24, and Nb30 were selected in vitro, with Nb30 demonstrating promising activity. Following engineering, the Nb30-1 variant was generated and shown to exhibit enhanced efficacy. In combination with colistin, Nb30-1 effectively inhibited the growth of colistin-resistant, MCR-1.1-expressing laboratory Escherichia coli BL21(DE3), as determined by the growth dynamics curve. Molecular docking analysis revealed the binding interactions between Nb30/Nb30-1 and the MCR-1.1 protein, and affinity measurements confirmed their high binding affinity for the MCR-1.1 antigen. Given the exquisite conservation of key catalytic residues and the epitope recognized by Nb30-1 across MCR-1 variants, Nb30-1 represents a promising macromolecular adjuvant strategy to overcome MCR-1-mediated resistance.IMPORTANCEThe escalating use of antibiotics has driven a global rise in antibiotic resistance, underscoring an urgent need for adjuvants that can restore the susceptibility of drug-resistant bacteria. In this study, we isolate anti-MCR-1 nanobodies from a phage-display library and evaluate their potential to restore colistin efficacy. Following engineering, the Nb30-1 variant was generated and shown to exhibit enhanced efficacy. These findings suggest that engineered anti-MCR-1 nanobodies, particularly Nb30-1, represent a promising therapeutic strategy to combat MCR-1-positive colistin-resistant bacterial infections by resensitizing bacteria to colistin.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Optimization of whole-cell human depletion provides increased sensitivity and microbial genome coverage from respiratory metagenomic assays.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Metagenomics is being adopted worldwide as a laboratory-developed test. We have previously reported a unified metagenomic method for the direct detection of microorganisms from respiratory samples, delivering preliminary results within 6 h with >90% sensitivity for both viral and bacterial pathogens. This has now been deployed across the United Kingdom National Health Service (NHS) through the NHS Respiratory Metagenomics Network. Since this deployment, we have identified a number of improvements to the method to further increase sensitivity. In this manuscript, we report these optimizations, including the addition of a bead-beating cycle, substitution of the endonuclease enzyme, and controlled termination of the endonuclease reaction. This updated protocol (v1.2) resulted in substantially improved assay performance. Validation in 6 NHS hospitals using both protocols in parallel (v1 and v1.2) with 107 clinical respiratory samples demonstrated increased bacterial and viral read recovery in v1.2, translating to higher pathogen genome coverage compared to v1. Overall, bacterial sensitivity for v1.2 was 98% compared to 93% for v1, and viral sensitivity was 90% for v1.2 compared to 80% for v1. This multicenter validation has confirmed reproducibility and scalability of the new protocol, establishing a robust framework for clinical implementation of metagenomics.IMPORTANCEThis work represents the validation of an important major update to the protocol used in the United Kingdom National Health Service (NHS) Respiratory Metagenomics service. The service is now deployed in six major hospitals across the UK, and the results of this multicenter validation, as well as showing improved sensitivity, confirm this is a method that is easy to operate and implement in existing hospital laboratories and still provide a same-day turnaround time. The importance of this work is that it provides another step forward to respiratory metagenomics becoming established as a routine clinical diagnostic method.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Genome-resolved multi-omics characterizes bacterial, viral, and metabolic components associated with Parkinson's disease gut ecosystem variation.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder involving the gut-brain axis, yet genome-resolved characterization of bacterial and viral communities with metabolic context remains limited. Here, we performed deep shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomic profiling in a high-altitude cohort comprising patients with PD and environmentally matched spouse controls (living at approximately 1,900 m altitude). We reconstructed 455 species-level genome bins (SGBs) and 2,957 non-redundant viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), enabling high-resolution profiling of bacterial and viral community composition. Rather than a uniform shift of the entire microbial community, PD-associated variation involved specific bacterial, viral, and metabolic components. Indicator analysis identified 23 bacterial and 86 viral candidate indicators associated with PD or control status, with predicted temperate phages representing the predominant lifestyle category among indicator vOTUs. Several PD-associated bacterial indicators included taxa previously linked to anaerobic fermentation and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-associated metabolism, accompanied by increased fecal valerate. Abundance correlation analysis identified covariation patterns between bacterial and viral indicators, including associations between controls (CK)-associated Agathobacter faecis and Lachnospiraceae-linked vOTUs. Integrating microbial abundance profiles and metabolomic measurements revealed exploratory associations among microbial indicators and metabolic alterations associated with PD. Cross-layer analyses further showed reduced dispersion of microbial-metabolomic alignment patterns in PD samples, suggesting a more constrained ecological state. Together, these findings provide a genome-resolved view of bacterial, viral, and metabolic variation in the PD gut ecosystem, extending characterization of PD-associated dysbiosis beyond bacterial taxonomy and identifying candidate microbial indicators and metabolic alterations for further investigation.IMPORTANCEParkinson's disease (PD) is a complex neurological disorder in which interactions between the host and the gut ecosystem are increasingly recognized as relevant to disease-associated biological processes. Previous microbiome studies of Parkinson's disease have largely focused on bacterial taxonomic changes, while gut viral communities and their relationships with microbial metabolism remain less characterized. In this study, we used genome-resolved metagenomics and metabolomics to characterize bacterial, viral, and metabolic components associated with PD in individuals with Parkinson's disease and environmentally matched controls. Our findings provide a broader view of Parkinson's disease-associated gut ecosystem alterations beyond bacterial composition alone, highlighting bacteriophages as an underexplored ecological component and identifying microbial indicators and metabolic alterations for future investigation.

Molecular Biology and Evolution.title: B-cell intrinsic Pax transactivation domain-interacting protein promotes intestinal inflammation by restraining B2 cell-mediated macrophage interleukin-10 responses
Molecular Biology and Evolution.abstract: AbstractBackground and aimsB cells are increasingly recognized as important regulators of intestinal inflammation through both antibody-dependent and antibody-independent mechanisms, but the intrinsic programs controlling inflammatory B-cell functions remain poorly understood. Pax transactivation domain-interacting protein (PTIP) is an essential regulator of B-cell humoral immunity; however, its role in inflammatory B-cell responses remains unclear.MethodsWe investigated the function of B-cell-intrinsic PTIP using B-cell-specific PTIP-deficient mice and dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced experimental colitis. Pax transactivation domain-interacting protein expression was evaluated in murine and human B cells, including analysis of a publicly available human colonic single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset. Antibody-mediated effects, B2-cell-intrinsic activity, and macrophage-associated responses were examined using adoptive transfer, serum transfer, macrophage depletion, and interleukin (IL)-10 pathway blockade approaches.ResultsPTIP expression was increased in circulating B cells from patients with inflammatory bowel disease and intestinal B cells during DSS-induced colitis. B-cell-specific PTIP deficiency attenuated colitis severity and reduced germinal center B-cell responses and immunoglobulin production. However, adoptive transfer and serum transfer experiments suggested that the protective effect of PTIP deficiency was largely independent of antibody-mediated mechanisms. Transfer of PTIP-deficient conventional B2 cells reduced intestinal inflammation, whereas PTIP-expressing B2 cells promoted disease severity, demonstrating a B2-cell intrinsic function of PTIP. Furthermore, PTIP deficiency enhanced macrophage-associated IL-10 responses, and disruption of macrophage function or IL-10 signaling diminished this protective phenotype.ConclusionsPTIP promotes DSS-induced intestinal inflammation by regulating antibody-independent B2-cell inflammatory activity and B2-cell–macrophage communication. These findings identify a previously unrecognized PTIP-dependent immune regulatory pathway linking B-cell intrinsic programs to macrophage-mediated intestinal inflammation.

Molecular Biology and Evolution.title: Efficacy and safety of microfragmented autologous adipose tissue transplantation for perianal fistulas in Crohn’s disease (ATTIC): a phase 3 multicenter randomized controlled trial
Molecular Biology and Evolution.abstract: AbstractBackground and AimsComplex perianal fistulas in Crohn’s disease are often refractory to the recommended combination of surgery and biological drug therapy. We investigated the efficacy and safety of minimally manipulated, microfragmented, autologous adipose tissue (“MFat”), after surgical debridement of the fistula, in patients with Crohn’s disease in whom standard treatments had failed.MethodsThis double-blind, randomized controlled trial enrolled 80 adults who all underwent cone-like partial fistulectomy of a complex fistula (one inner orifice and up to three external openings) followed by either MFat injection or suture of the inner orifice and saline injection. MFat was prepared from lipoaspirates using Lipogems medical devices immediately before fistulectomy and transplanted around the inner orifice and along the residual tracts immediately after fistulectomy. The primary efficacy outcome was combined (clinicoradiological) remission at 24 weeks in the per-protocol populations. Safety was assessed in the all-patients-treated populations.ResultsAfter randomization, 37 patients in each group were treated and 33 patients each were assessed. Combined remission occurred in 19 patients (57.6%) of the intervention group and six control patients (18.2%) (risk ratio 3.17; 95% CI, 1.45-6.91; P = .004; number needed to treat, 3). Clinical remission was found in 26 (78.8%) and 18 (54.5%) patients, respectively (P = .044), while clinical indices improved in both groups. Seven adverse events were reported, without significant differences between groups in safety endpoints.ConclusionsPartial fistulectomy alone led to substantial clinical improvement, but the addition of MFat significantly increased the likelihood of achieving MRI-confirmed healing. Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05594862).

mSystems.title: High-resolution transcriptome analysis reveals a multilayered and dynamic transcriptional architecture in the archaeal virus SSV1.
mSystems.abstract: Members of Fuselloviridae infecting thermoacidophilic Sulfolobales are among the best-studied archaeal viruses, with the Saccharolobus spindle-shaped virus 1 (SSV1)-Saccharolobus solfataricus interaction serving as a model system. After infection, SSV1 establishes a chronic infection with new virions continuously budding from the infected cell. UV irradiation triggers virus replication, increased virion production, and a tightly orchestrated temporal transcription cycle. However, gene regulatory mechanisms post-UV induction remain elusive. In this study, we investigated the SSV1 transcriptomic landscape post-UV induction using high-resolution, long-read Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) cappable RNA sequencing. Through end-to-end sequencing of primary transcripts, we generated a comprehensive transcript map of SSV1, identifying 21 transcription start sites (TSSs), including 12 newly described sites, and 19 termination sites (TTSs), of which 9 are novel. This enabled refinement of transcription units and operon structures across the genome. Five new start sites of antisense transcription were discovered, including one antisense to the open reading frame of a putative viral toxin gene a291, which we hypothesize to be a cis-encoded regulatory RNA. In addition, spontaneous recombination between two direct repeats in the SSV1 structural genes vp1 and vp3 was confirmed. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation of cappable-seq for an archaeal virus and the first base-resolution analysis of the SSV1 transcriptome. It reveals a previously unappreciated level of transcriptional complexity, illustrating how high-resolution transcriptomics can deepen understanding of viral transcriptome architecture and regulatory networks.IMPORTANCEArchaeal viruses remain among the least understood viruses in the virosphere, despite their ecological and evolutionary significance. Saccharolobus spindle-shaped virus 1 (SSV1) is a key model for the study of virus-host interactions in archaea. Yet, its gene regulatory mechanisms have remained poorly resolved. Here, we provide the first base-pair resolution transcriptome of an archaeal virus, revealing a complex and multi-layered transcriptional architecture. We uncover alternative transcription start and termination sites, as well as antisense transcription, pointing to regulatory mechanisms beyond a simple temporal gene expression program. These findings suggest that archaeal viruses use sophisticated transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms similar to those in bacterial and eukaryotic viruses. By establishing a high-resolution map of the SSV1 transcriptome, this work advances our understanding of archaeal virus biology.
