Obesity is associated with alterations in the composition and function of the gut microbiota in patients with obstructive sleep apnea.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder marked by upper airway collapse, intermittent hypoxia, and sleep disruption. Growing evidence links gut microbiota dysbiosis to OSA-related complications, with obesity as a key risk factor. This study investigates the associations of OSA and obesity status with gut microbiota characteristics. Fecal samples were collected from 65 OSA patients and 15 healthy controls (HCs) and analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Clinical parameters, including body mass index (BMI), apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), lowest oxygen saturation (LSaO2), mean oxygen saturation (MSaO₂), and cumulative time with oxygen saturation below 90% (CT90), were also collected. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) analysis, random forest, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression were employed to identify key microbial genera associated with OSA and obesity. Within the OSA cohort, subjects were stratified by BMI into obese OSA (Ob + OSA) and non-obese OSA (Non + OSA) groups to evaluate the association between obesity and the gut microbiota of OSA patients. The gut microbiota of OSA patients exhibited significant differences from that of healthy controls in terms of both community diversity and composition. LEfSe analysis, along with random forest and LASSO regression analyses, revealed a significant enrichment of Blautia, Fusobacterium, and the Eubacterium hallii group in OSA patients, while the abundance of Faecalibacterium was significantly reduced. Functional prediction analysis further indicated significantly enhanced activity in lipid metabolism and digestive system functions in OSA patients compared with healthy controls. Obese OSA (Ob + OSA) patients displayed differences in alpha diversity and the relative abundance of specific microbial taxa compared to non-obese OSA (Non + OSA) patients. The abundance of Synergistota was significantly higher in the Ob + OSA group than in the Non + OSA group, whereas the abundance of Blautia and Bifidobacterium was significantly lower. LEfSe analysis and LASSO regression identified increased Acidaminococcus, Megasphaera, and Morganella and decreased Anaerostipes and Lachnospiraceae UCG-004 as key characteristic genera distinguishing Ob + OSA from Non + OSA. Furthermore, obese patients exhibited more active functional pathways related to the metabolism of terpenoids and polyketides. The gut microbiota of OSA patients markedly differs from that of healthy controls, with obesity being associated with differences in microbial composition. Genera such as Blautia, the Eubacterium hallii group, and Faecalibacterium may serve as potential biomarkers for OSA, while Acidaminococcus, Megasphaera, Morganella, Anaerostipes, and Lachnospiraceae UCG-004 are characteristic of obese OSA patients. These microbial alterations may contribute to OSA pathogenesis and progression. This study provides further insight into gut microbial heterogeneity among OSA patients with different obesity statuses and provides a basis for future prospective and mechanistic studies. [IMPORTANCE] This study investigated gut microbiota characteristics in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) according to their obesity status and compared these findings with those in healthy controls. By comparing obese and non-obese patients within the OSA cohort, we identified differences in microbial diversity and the relative abundance of specific taxa associated with obesity status. These findings provide further evidence of heterogeneity in the gut microbiota among OSA patients with different obesity statuses and may help inform future studies investigating the relationships among obesity, OSA, and the gut microbiota.

mSystems.title: A multi-layer, multi-species graph-based framework for comparative analysis of sRNA-mediated regulation.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Small RNAs (sRNAs) are central post-transcriptional regulators of bacterial gene expression, yet their evolutionary dynamics remain difficult to resolve due to limited sequence conservation. While sequence-homologous sRNAs can retain or diverge in function, unrelated sRNAs may independently evolve to regulate similar biological processes, making functional conservation invisible to sequence-based approaches. Here, we present a multi-layer, multi-species graph-based framework that integrates experimentally detected sRNA-messenger RNA interactions, orthology relationships, functional annotations, and semantic clustering of Gene Ontology biological process terms. The framework provides two complementary tools for assessing functional conservation among orthologous sRNAs and convergent regulation by distinct sRNAs across species, capturing functional signals that are weak in individual data sources, yet emerge from integrating multiple layers and species. Applied to six Gammaproteobacterial strains, our approach reveals that functional conservation is frequently maintained among orthologous sRNAs despite divergence in their target repertoires. We further identify lineage-specific regulatory modules and cases of convergent regulation, where non-homologous sRNAs from phylogenetically distant species independently regulate the same essential biological processes. These results demonstrate that sRNA-mediated regulation is both evolutionarily flexible and functionally constrained. The framework is modular, scalable, and adaptable to additional data sets and regulatory layers, establishing a generalizable and hypothesis-generating approach for studying the evolution of post-transcriptional regulatory networks across species. [IMPORTANCE] Small RNAs (sRNAs) help bacteria rapidly adjust gene expression in response to changing environments, yet understanding how these regulators evolve across species remains challenging. Sequence similarity alone often provides an incomplete picture because related sRNAs can diverge in function, while unrelated sRNAs may independently regulate the same biological processes. We developed a computational framework that compares sRNA regulatory function across multiple bacterial species by integrating regulatory interactions, evolutionary relationships, and functional annotations. Applied to six bacterial strains, the framework revealed that many sRNAs maintain similar biological roles despite extensive changes in their target genes. It also uncovered cases in which distinct, non-homologous sRNAs independently regulate the same essential processes, including iron acquisition, stress responses, and central metabolism. These findings provide new insights into the evolution of bacterial regulatory networks and establish an open-source resource for comparative analysis of post-transcriptional regulation across diverse species.
